Details of Public Law 119-64, section 2, Disaster Related Extension of Deadlines Act

Title
Disaster Related Extension of Deadlines Act, Postponement of certain deadlines by reason of disasters made applicable to limitation on credit or refund
Fed Effective Date
12/26/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to claims for credit or refunds filed, and collection notices issued, after 12/26/2025.
Background
Disaster Related Extension of Deadlines Act
IRC Section
6303, 7508A
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
18572, 19033-19034, 19041, 19057-19061, 19063, 19065-19066, 19066.5, 19067, 19306, 19308, 19311, 19311.5, 19312-19314, 19316, 19322.1
Summary of Federal Change

IRC Section 7508A

Generally, when a tax return is timely filed, a claim for credit or refund may be filed up to three years from the date filed. Federal law (IRC section 7508A) allows certain administrative disaster tax relief, such as postponement of filing and payment deadlines, once a federal disaster is declared by the President. The postponement provisions provided under IRC 7508A did not apply to the period of time a taxpayer is allowed to file a claim for credit or refund.

The provision provides that for qualified taxpayers affected by federally declared disaster, significant fire, or terroristic or military actions any extension of time provided to taxpayers to file their tax return would also apply to the statute of limitations to file for a credit or claim for refund (IRC 6511).

IRC Section 6303

Federal law provides that taxpayers are informed of taxes due within 60 days from the date assessed. If a tax is assessed prior to the last date for payment of tax, payment of tax is not demanded until after such date.

The provision provides that, for qualified taxpayers affected by federally declared disaster, significant fire, or terroristic or military actions, the last date for payment of any tax will be extended by the period provided under IRC 7508A for purposes of mailing a notice and demanding tax.

California Impact

California conforms to IRC 7508A, as of the specified date January 1, 2025, with modifications, relating to postponement of certain tax-related deadlines. Under California law, the Director of Finance has the authority to determine whether a taxpayer is affected by a state of emergency, and whether state tax deadlines should be postponed due to a federally declared disaster, significant fire, or a terroristic or military action disaster. California law provides impacted taxpayers with postponement of state tax-related deadlines an additional relief period, that begins on the date the state postponement period expires, if any, and ends on the date the federal postponement period expires if requested by the taxpayer.

California law does not conform to the modifications made by this section of the public law. California law provides that taxpayers can file a claim for refund four years from the earlier of the due date of the tax return or the date filed, or one year from the date of the overpayment, whichever is later.

California does not conform to the federal notice and demand for tax but has a standalone law under the Administration of Franchise and Income Tax Law.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70101, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Extension and enhancement of reduced rates
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
1
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17041
Summary of Federal Change

This provision makes permanent the tax rate structure established under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 11001) that was set to expire on December 31, 2025. For taxable year 2025, the rates are as follows:

  • 10% for incomes of single individuals with incomes of $11,925 or less ($23,850 for married couples filing jointly)
  • 12% for incomes over $11,925 ($23,850 for married couples filing jointly)
  • 22% for incomes over $48,475 ($96,950 for married couples filing jointly)
  • 24% for incomes over $103,350 ($206,700 for married couples filing jointly)
  • 32% for incomes over $197,300 ($394,600 for married couples filing jointly)
  • 35% for incomes over $250,525 ($501,050 for married couples filing jointly
  • 37% for individual single taxpayers with incomes greater than $626,350 ($751,600 for married couples filing jointly).

The 10 percent and 12 percent tax rate brackets would be indexed for inflation using the 2016 Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (C–CPI–U) beginning after December 31, 2025. The remaining tax brackets would use the 2017 C-CPI-U.

The provision also makes the capital gains and losses breakpoints permanent. Therefore, in the case of an individual (including an estate or trust) with adjusted net capital gain, to the extent the gain would not result in taxable income exceeding the 15 percent breakpoint, such gain is not taxed. Any adjusted net capital gain which would result in taxable income exceeding the 15 percent breakpoint but not exceeding the 20 percent breakpoint is taxed at 15 percent. The remaining adjusted net capital gain is taxed at 20 percent.

California Impact

California does not conform, under PITL, to federal individual income tax rates, and instead has its own individual income tax rates that range from 1 percent to 12.3 percent. In addition, there is an additional tax of 1 percent on the portion of a taxpayer’s taxable income that exceeds $1,000,000. Thus, the maximum personal income tax rate is 13.3 percent.

California conforms, under the PITL and the CTL, to the federal rules for computing capital gains and losses, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications. However, California does not provide special tax rates for net capital gain; instead, such gains are taxed at the same rates as ordinary income.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70102, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Extension and enhancement of increased standard deduction
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2024.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
63
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17073, 17073.5, and 17304
Summary of Federal Change

The provision makes permanent the increased standard deduction amounts established under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 11021) for individuals across all filing statuses. Under the provision, the amount of the standard deduction applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, is $31,500 for married individuals filing a joint return, $23,625 for head-of-household filers, and $15,750 for all other taxpayers.

The amount of the standard deduction is indexed for inflation using the Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (C–CPI–U) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.

California Impact

California does not conform to the federal standard deduction, but instead has stand-alone law allowing a California standard deduction in lieu of the federal standard deduction, as follows:

Filing Status 2025 California Standard Deduction Amounts
Single or married/registered domestic partner (RDP) filing separately: $5,706
Marred/RDP filing jointly, head of household, or qualifying widow(er): $11,412
The minimum standard deduction for dependents: $1,350

Nonresidents and part-year residents are allowed a standard deduction in the above amounts as modified by the ratio that California AGI bears to total AGI (not to exceed 100 percent).

Revenue Impact
N/A

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70103, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Termination of deduction for personal exemptions other than temporary senior deduction
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2024.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
151, 6213
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17054, 17054.1, 19051
Summary of Federal Change

This provision makes permanent the repeal of the deduction for personal exemptions established under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 11041).

Additionally, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, and before January 1, 2029, this provision allows a deduction in amount equal to $6,000 for each qualified individual. The deduction is reduced for taxpayers whose modified adjusted gross income (AGI) exceeds $75,000 ($150,000 for married filing joint).

The provision defines the term “qualified individual” as the taxpayer, if the taxpayer has attained age 65 before the close of the taxable year, and in the case of a joint return, the taxpayer’s spouse, if such spouse has attained age 65 before the close of the taxable year.

To claim the senior deduction, the taxpayer must have a valid social security number (SSN) on the return for the taxable year. The omission of a valid SSN will be treated as a mathematical or clerical error. Additionally, in the case of a married individual, they must file a joint return to claim the deduction.

California Impact

California does not conform to federal personal-exemption deductions. Instead of personal-exemption deductions, the PITL provides personal-exemption tax credits, including a senior exemption for individuals age 65 or older. For taxable years 2025, individual taxpayers are allowed personal-exemption tax credits in the amounts shown below:

Exemption Type Number of Exemptions Exemption Amount
Personal Exemption One exemption for themselves, and one for a spouse, if married filing joint (MFJ): $153
Senior One additional exemption if 65 or older, and one for a spouse 65 or older, if MFJ: $153
Blind One additional exemption if visually impaired and one for a visually impaired spouse: $153
Dependent One exemption for each qualifying dependent: $475

The personal-exemption tax credits are reduced when a taxpayer’s federal AGI exceeds a threshold amount. For taxable year 2025, the exemption credits are reduced by $6 ($12 if married filing joint) for each $2,500 ($1,250 if married filing separately) of AGI or fraction thereof, that exceeds the following threshold amounts:

  • Single or Married/RDP filing separate — $252,203
  • Married/RDP filing joint — $504,411
  • Head of Household — $378,310

Under the Administration of Franchise and Income Tax Law (AFITL), FTB treats specified errors identified on the return during processing as math errors, which includes not providing a valid identification number as required to claim a dependent exemption tax credit, earned income tax credit, young child tax credit, or foster youth tax credit. California doesn’t conform to the definition of mathematical or clerical error under IRC section 6213. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision related to IRC section 6213.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70104, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Extension and enhancement of increased child tax credit
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2024.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
24, 6213
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
19051
Summary of Federal Change

The provision makes permanent the child tax credit modifications established under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 11022). For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, the amount of child tax credit is increased to $2,200 per qualifying child. The credit is further modified to permanently provide for a $500 nonrefundable credit for qualifying dependents other than qualifying children. The provision generally retains the present-law definition of dependent.

Under the provision, the maximum amount of the credit that is refundable may not exceed $1,400 per qualifying child. The maximum amount of the credit that is refundable is indexed for inflation using the Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (C–CPI–U) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Additionally, the provision provides that, in order to receive the child tax credit (i.e., both the refundable and non-refundable portion), a taxpayer must include a social security number (SSN) for each qualifying child for whom the credit is claimed on the tax return. For these purposes, an SSN must be issued before the due date for the filing of the return for the taxable year.

Further, the provision retains the present-law age limit for a qualifying child. Thus, a qualifying child is an individual who has not attained age 17 during the taxable year.

Finally, the provision makes permanent the modified adjusted gross income phaseout thresholds. The credit begins to phase out for taxpayers with adjusted gross income in excess of $400,000 (in the case of married taxpayers filing a joint return) and $200,000 (for all other taxpayers). These phaseout thresholds are not indexed for inflation.

The amount of the child tax credit is indexed for inflation using the C–CPI–U for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.

To claim the child tax credit, the taxpayer must have a valid social security number on the return for the taxable year. Additionally, the SSN must be issued to a citizen of the United States. The omission of a valid SSN will be treated as a mathematical or clerical error.

California Impact

California does not conform to the child tax credit under IRC section 24 and has no comparable credit.

California has a refundable Young Child Tax Credit (YCTC). The YCTC is allowed to an eligible individual who has been allowed the California Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), has at least one qualifying child for the EITC, and has one qualifying child under the age of six years old as of the last day of the year. The maximum amount of the refundable credit is $1,000 and phases in at $25,000 of earned income and phases out at $30,000.

Under the Administration of Franchise and Income Tax Law (AFITL), FTB treats specified errors identified on the return during processing as math errors, which includes not providing a valid identification number as required to claim a dependent exemption tax credit, earned income tax credit, young child tax credit, or foster youth tax credit. California doesn’t conform to the definition of mathematical or clerical error under IRC section 6213. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision related to IRC section 6213.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70105, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Extension and enhancement of deduction for qualified business income
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
199A
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17201.6
Summary of Federal Change

The provision makes permanent the 20 percent deduction for qualified business income (QBI), established under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 11011), which would have expired on December 31, 2025. In addition, the minimum deduction for QBI is set to $400.

The provision also increases phase-in threshold amount on taxable income based on W-2 wages paid and capital from $50,000 to $75,000 ($100,000 to $150,000 in the case of a joint return). A disallowance of the deduction with respect to specified service trades or businesses is also phased in above the threshold amount of taxable income.

The provision defines the term “applicable taxpayer” as a taxpayer whose aggregate qualified business income with respect to all active qualified trades or businesses of the taxpayer for such taxable year is at least $1,000.

The provision defines the term “active qualified trade or business” as any qualified trade or business of the taxpayer in which the taxpayer materially participates (within the meaning of IRC section 469(h)).

The amount for both the QBI minimum deduction and applicable taxpayer’s aggregate qualified business income are indexed for inflation using the Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (C–CPI–U) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2026.

California Impact

California does not conform, under the PITL, to the federal deduction for qualified business income of pass-through entities under IRC section 199A.

Revenue Impact

The estimated revenue impact to conform to the above provisions would result in the following loss:

26/27 27/28 28/29 29/30
$(5,000,000,000) $(3,500,000,000) $(3,600,000,000) $(3,700,000,000)

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70106, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Extension and enhancement of increased estate and gift tax exemption amounts
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
2010
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17062
Summary of Federal Change

The provision makes permanent the estate and gift tax exemption amounts for estates of decedents dying and gifts made, established under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 11061), made after December 31, 2025. This is accomplished by increasing the basic exclusion amount (IRC section 2010(c)(3)) from $5 million to $15 million.

Summary of Federal Change

This provision makes permanent the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act provision (Public Law 115-97, section 11044), that was set to expire on December 31, 2025, limiting the itemized deduction for personal casualty or theft loss to only those losses attributable to a Federally declared disaster. This provision expands the itemized deduction for losses if they were attributable to a State declared disaster.

This provision adds and defines the term “State declared disaster”, as any natural catastrophe which includes any hurricane, tornado, storm, high water, wind-driven water, tidal wave, tsunami, earthquake, volcanic eruption, landslide, mudslide, snowstorm, drought, or, regardless of cause, any fire, flood, or explosion, in any part of the State. The Governor of such state will make the determination with the Secretary of the Treasury whether the natural catastrophe causes damage of sufficient severity and magnitude to warrant the application of this rule.

California Impact

Under the PITL, California conforms to the treatment of personal casualty loss deductions under IRC section 165(h), as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications and specifically does not conform to the federal modification to only allow a deduction for presidentially declared or State declared disasters as personal casualty losses.

California tax law identifies specific events as disasters and excess disaster losses are allowed special carry forward treatment. That is, 100 percent of the excess disaster loss may be carried over for up to 15 taxable years. In addition, IRC section 165(i), relating to the election to take a loss deduction in the preceding year, applies to disasters that were the subject of a Governor’s proclamation, but not the subject of a Presidential disaster declaration.

As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

Title

California Conforms?

Summary of Federal Change

This provision modifies the overall limitation on itemized deductions that was paused under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 11046).

Under this provision, the total allowable amount of itemized deductions is reduced by 2/37 of the lesser of:

  • the total allowable amount of itemized deductions for the taxable year or
  • the taxpayer’s amount of taxable income, without regards to this section and increased by the itemized deductions, that exceeds the dollar amount at which the 37% tax bracket applies to the taxpayer.

The provision no longer carves out deductions for medical expenses, investment interest, and casualty, theft or gambling losses from the limitation.

This provision also excludes the limitation on the total allowable amount of itemized deductions for purposes of determining the qualified business income deduction, which allows a taxpayer, other than a corporation, to deduct for any taxable year an amount equal to the lesser of the taxpayer’s combined qualified business income amount or an amount equal to 20 percent of the excess (if any) of the taxpayer’s taxable income over the net capital gain of the taxable year (IRC section 199A).

California Impact

Under the PTIL, California conforms to the overall limitation on itemized deductions as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications, but does not conform to this federal modification of the overall limitation on itemized deductions.

California phases out itemized deductions for taxpayers whose AGI exceeds certain thresholds. For 2025, the amount of otherwise allowable itemized deductions (other than medical expenses, investment interest, casualty, theft, or wagering losses) is reduced by the lesser of:

  • Six percent of the amount of the taxpayer’s AGI in excess of $252,203 for single or married-filing-separate/RDP taxpayers, $504,411 for married/RDP taxpayers filing a joint return, and $378,310 for taxpayers who file under the head-of-household status, or
  • 80 percent of the amount of the itemized deductions otherwise allowable for such taxable year.

Under the PITL, California does not conform to the federal deduction for qualified business income under IRC section 199A.

As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

Summary of Federal Change

The IRC provides for a tax-favored savings program intended to benefit disabled individuals, known as qualified ABLE programs. The provision makes permanent the increased contribution limitation to ABLE accounts under certain circumstances, which was set to expire under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law (P.L.) 115-97, section 11024(a)), for contributions made before January 1, 2026.

While the general overall limitation on contributions (the per-donee annual gift tax exclusion ($19,000 for 2025)) remains the same, the limitation is increased with respect to contributions made by the designated beneficiary of the ABLE account. Under the provision, after the overall limitation on contributions is reached, an ABLE account’s designated beneficiary may contribute an additional amount, up to the lesser of (a) the Federal poverty line for a one-person household; or (b) the individual’s compensation for the taxable year.

In addition, the new federal law extended the date for all other eligible qualified retirement contributions, for the credit, from before January 1, 2026, to before January 1, 2027. Impacted contributions include (1) elective deferrals to an IRC section 401(k) plan, an IRC section 403(b) plan, a governmental IRC section 457 plan, a SIMPLE plan, or a SARSEP; (2) contributions to a traditional or Roth IRA; and (3) voluntary after-tax employee contributions to a qualified retirement plan or IRC section 403(b) plan.

The provision makes permanent the change under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 11026), which granted combat zone tax benefits to the Sinai Peninsula of Egypt if, as of the date of enactment of the provision, any member of the Armed Forces of the United States is entitled to special pay under section 310 of title 37, United States Code (relating to special pay; duty subject to hostile fire or imminent danger), for services performed in such location. A qualified hazardous duty area is defined as Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, or Macedonia if, as of March 20, 1996, any member of the Armed Forces of the United States is entitled to certain special pay provisions, relating to duty subject to hostile fire or imminent danger, for services performed in that country. However, California does not conform to the new federal provisions that define the Sinai Peninsula of Egypt, Kenya, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Chad as qualified hazardous duty areas.

Summary of Federal Change

The provision permanently provides a gross income exclusion for certain loan amounts that are discharged on account of death or disability after December 31, 2025. The exclusion was set to expire on December 31, 2025, as established under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law (P.L.) 115-97, section 11031) and American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 (P.L. 117-2, section 9675). Student loans that continue to be eligible for the exclusion are loans made by (1) the United States (or an instrumentality or agency thereof), (2) a State (or any political subdivision thereof), (3) certain tax-exempt public benefit corporations that control a State, county, or municipal hospital and whose employees have been deemed to be public employees under State law, (4) an educational organization which normally maintains a regular faculty and curriculum and normally has a regularly enrolled body of pupils or students in attendance at the place where its educational activities are regularly carried on, and includes refinanced loans, (5) an organization exempt from tax under IRC section 501(a) for refinanced loans, or (6) private education loans (for this purpose, private education loan is defined in section 140(a) of the Consumer Protection Act).

The discharge of a loan as described above is excluded from gross income if the discharge was pursuant to the death or total and permanent disability of the student.

To be eligible for the income exclusion for discharged student loans, the taxpayer must have a valid social security number on the return for the taxable year. The omission of a valid social security number will be treated as a mathematical or clerical error.

California Impact

California generally conforms, under the PITL, to the federal income tax rules relating to the cancellation of student loans under IRC section 108, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications explained below.

In 2019, Assembly Bill 91 was chaptered to conform to Section 11031(a) of P.L. 115-97, relating to the income exclusion for loan discharges on account of death or total and permanent disability and applies to discharges of indebtedness after December 31, 2018. As a result, California conforms to the changes made by this provision for the gross income exclusion for student loan discharges due to the death or disability of the debtor for discharges after December 31, 2025, but does not conform to the change requiring the taxpayer to have a valid social security number on the return for the taxable year.

Additionally, regarding the omission of a taxpayer’s social security number, California has stand-alone law. Under the Administration of Franchise and Income Tax Law, FTB treats specified errors identified on the return during processing as math errors, which includes not providing a valid identification number as required to claim a dependent exemption tax credit, earned income tax credit, young child tax credit, or foster your tax credit.

Summary of Federal Change

The provision permanently limits the amount allowed as an itemized deduction for the aggregate amount of state and local, etc. taxes. Under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law (P.L.) 115-97, section 11042), the deduction was limited up to $10,000 ($5,000 for married taxpayers filing a separate return) and applied to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2017, and beginning before January 1, 2026. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (P.L. 117-169, section 13904) also extended the limitation to taxable years ending before January 1, 2027.

Beginning in taxable year 2025, the provision modifies the annual limitation for the aggregate amount of deductible taxes as follows:

  • For taxable year 2025, $40,000.
  • For taxable year 2026, $40,400.
  • For taxable years 2027 through taxable year 2029, the aggregate amount is adjusted by 1 percent each taxable year with taxable year 2026 as the base year.
  • For taxable year 2030 and after, $10,000.

Additionally, for taxable year 2025 through taxable year 2029, to determine the applicable limit, the provision requires a phasedown adjustment and is based on modified adjusted gross income (MAGI). The applicable limit is reduced by 30 percent of the excess of the taxpayer’s MAGI over the threshold amount (half the threshold amount in the case of a married individual filing a separate return). The threshold amount is $500,000 for taxable years 2025 and 2026, and is increased each year by 1 percent from the prior year, until 2030. This provision defines MAGI as the adjusted gross income of the taxpayer plus certain income earned or sourced outside of the United States that is excluded from gross income.

The provision provides that the phasedown adjustment cannot result in an applicable limitation amount that is less than $10,000.

California Impact

California conforms, under the PITL, to the deductibility of certain taxes and other provisions related to the deductibility of taxes under IRC section 164, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications. Specifically, California does not allow a deduction for state or local income taxes. California does not conform to the limited deduction applicable to individuals for state and local real and personal property taxes and state, local, and foreign income, war profits, and excess profits taxes for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

The deduction is reduced for taxpayers whose modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) exceeds $150,000 ($300,000 for married filing joint). This provision also allows this deduction in addition to the standard deduction for taxpayers who do not itemize.

This provision defines “qualified tips” as cash paid, or amounts charged, including amounts received by an employee under any tip sharing arrangement in an occupation that receives tips on a customary and regular basis. Qualified tips do not include amounts that are not provided voluntarily, not in a specified service trade or business, or excluded under guidance to be established by the Secretary.

This provision requires a valid Social Security Number (SSN) to be provided on the return to claim the deduction. An omission of the correct SSN on the return is treated as a math or clerical error. Additionally, in the case of a married individual, they must file a joint return to claim the deduction.

This provision excludes amounts deducted under this provision from the definition of qualified business income. This provision expands the types of businesses that can take the credit for employer social security taxes paid to include beauty services, such as barbering and hair care, nail care, esthetics, and body and spa treatments, where tipping is customary.

This provision requires information reporting by employers to the Secretary of the Treasury and to the employee on the tip income received and occupation of the employee on information returns and statements furnished to the taxpayer.

This provision requires the Secretary of the Treasury, no later than 90 days after the enactment of this Act, to publish a list of occupations that regularly and customarily received tips on or before December 31, 2024. The Secretary is required to modify the withholding calculations to include the new deduction.

California Impact

California conforms, under the PITL, to the definition of taxable income under IRC section 63, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications. California does not conform to the federal standard deduction amounts but instead has its own standard-deduction law. Nonresidents and part-year residents are allowed a standard deduction as modified by the ratio that California AGI bears to total AGI (not to exceed 100 percent). California generally conforms, under the PITL, to additional itemized deductions, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications. The changes made to federal law by this provision were added after January 1, 2025. As a result, California does not conform to the deduction for tips received.

Additionally, California does not conform to the federal deduction for qualified business income of pass-through entities under IRC section 199A. As a result, California does not conform to the exclusion of the amount of tips that a deduction is allowed from “qualified business income” for the purposes of the qualified business income deduction.

Under the Administration of Franchise and Income Tax Law (AFITL), the Franchise Tax Board (FTB) may require a copy of any information return required to be filed with the Secretary of the Treasury, at the time, and in the form and manner as the FTB may, by forms and instructions, require . As a result, California would conform to the changes requiring the information return related to the tip income received and occupation of the employee.

Additionally, under the AFITL, FTB treats specified errors identified on the return during processing as math errors, which includes not providing a valid identification number as required to claim a dependent exemption tax credit, earned income tax credit, young child tax credit, or foster your tax credit. California does not conform to the definition of mathematical or clerical error under IRC section 6213. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision related to IRC section 6213.

California does not conform to the employer credit for social security taxes under IRC section 45B. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made to this provision.

Annually, FTB is required to provide the EDD with wage withholding tables to be used by employers to withhold taxes on wages paid to their employees. The tables are based on the estimated amount of tax due on the wages paid by the employer. FTB does not conform to the requirement to modify withholding calculations under IRC section 3402.

Summary of Federal Change

This provision would allow a deduction of an amount equal to qualified overtime compensation received during the taxable year, not to exceed $12,500 ($25,000 for married filing joint), for taxable years beginning on or after December 31, 2024, and before January 1, 2029. Qualified overtime must be reported on information returns and statements furnished to the taxpayer. The deduction is reduced by $100 for each $1,000 by which the taxpayer’s modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) exceeds $150,000 ($300,000 in the case of a joint return). This provision also allows this deduction in addition to the standard deduction for taxpayers who do not itemize.

This provision defines “qualified overtime compensation” as overtime compensation paid to an individual as required under section 7 of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 that exceeds the regular rate of paid to the employed individual. Qualified overtime compensation does not include any qualified tips.

This provision requires a valid social security number (SSN) to be provided on the tax return to claim the deduction. An omission of the correct SSN on the return is treated as a math or clerical error. Additionally, in the case of a married individual, they must file a joint return to claim the deduction.

This provision requires information reporting by employers to the Secretary of the Treasury and to the employee on the amount of overtime compensation paid to the employee on W-2. Additionally, payors must provide this information to non-employees on Form 1099. The Secretary is required to modify the withholding calculations to include the new deduction.

California Impact

California conforms, under the PITL, to the definition of taxable income under IRC section 63, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications. California does not conform to the federal standard deduction amounts but instead has its own standard-deduction law. Nonresidents and part-year residents are allowed a standard deduction as modified by the ratio that California AGI bears to total AGI (not to exceed 100 percent). California generally conforms, under the PITL, to additional itemized deductions, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications. The changes made to federal law by this provision were added after January 1, 2025. As a result, California does not conform to the deduction for the overtime paid.

Under the Administration of Franchise and Income Tax Law (AFITL), the Franchise Tax Board (FTB) may require a copy of any information return required to be filed with the Secretary of the Treasury, at the time and in the form and manner as the FTB may, by forms and instructions, require. As a result, California would conform to the changes requiring the information return related to the amount of overtime compensation paid to the employee on W-2.

Additionally, under the AFITL, FTB treats specified errors identified on the return during processing as math errors, which includes not providing a valid identification number as required to claim a dependent exemption tax credit, earned income tax credit, young child tax credit, or foster youth tax credit. California doesn’t conform to the definition of mathematical or clerical error under IRC section 6213. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision related to IRC section 6213.

Annually, FTB is required to provide the EDD with wage withholding tables to be used by employers to withhold taxes on wages paid to their employees. The tables are based on the estimated amount of tax due on the wages paid by the employer. FTB does not conform to the requirement to modify withholding calculations under IRC section 3402.

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70203, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, No tax on car loan interest
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to indebtedness incurred after 12/31/2024.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
63, 163, 6050AA, 6724
California Conforms?
No, with respect to the deduction for car loan interest.
Yes, with respect to the information return provisions.
Relevant RTC Sections
17073, 17073.5, 17201, 17304, 18501, 18631, 19183
Summary of Federal Change

This provision allows a deduction up to $10,000 for interest paid or accrued on a qualified passenger vehicle loan for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, and before January 1, 2029. The deduction is reduced by $200 for every $1,000 (or portion of) by which the modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) exceeds $100,000 ($200,000 for married filing joint). This provision also allows this deduction in addition to the standard deduction for taxpayers who do not itemize.

This provision defines “qualified passenger vehicle loan interest” as interest paid or accrued during the taxable year on indebtedness incurred by the taxpayer after December 31, 2024, which is secured as a first lien or on a refinanced loan on an applicable passenger vehicle used for personal use. The deduction cannot be used for interest paid or incurred on a loan to finance fleet sales, commercial vehicles not used for personal use, lease financing, a vehicle with a salvage title, or a vehicle intended to be used for scrap or parts.

The deduction would also be allowed for a refinanced loan if the indebtedness is secured by a first lien on the applicable vehicle but only to the extent the indebtedness does not exceed the amount of the refinanced indebtedness. In addition, the deduction is not allowed for indebtedness owed to a related party.

The provision defines “applicable passenger vehicle” as a car, minivan, van, sports utility vehicle, pickup truck, or motorcycle used on public streets, roads, and highways. The vehicle’s original use must begin with the taxpayer. The vehicle must have at least two wheels, be treated as a motor vehicle under the Clean Air Act and has a gross vehicle weight rating of less than 14,000 pounds. The vehicle’s final assembly must take place in the U.S., where the vehicle is produced at or through the use of a plant, factory, or other place where it is delivered to a dealer with all components permanently installed or not necessary to operate the vehicle.

The deduction is not allowed unless the vehicle identification number (VIN) of the qualified passenger vehicle tis included on the individual’s tax return. This provision requires information reporting by any person who is engaged in a trade or business and through the business receives interest aggregating $600 or more for any calendar year on a passenger vehicle loan to report to the Secretary of the Treasury on the amount of interest received. Additionally, any person required to report to the Secretary of the Treasury must provide this information to taxpayers on an information return. A penalty would apply for failure to file a return reporting passenger vehicle loan interest and for failure to provide a payee statement to the taxpayer, unless the failure to file is due to reasonable cause and not willful neglect.

California Impact

California generally conforms, under the personal income tax law (PITL), to additional itemized deductions, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications. The changes made to federal law by this provision were added after January 1, 2025. As a result, California does not conform to the deduction for passenger vehicle loan interest.

Under the Administration of Franchise and Income Tax Law (AFITL), the FTB may require a copy of any information return required to be filed with the Secretary of the Treasury, that is added to the IRC by a public law enacted on or after January 1, 2009, at the time and in the form and manner as the FTB may, by forms and instructions, require. As a result, California would conform to the provision requiring the information return related to the passenger vehicle loan.

California generally conforms to IRC section 6724 for reasonable cause waiver, definition, and special rules, as of January 1, 2025, with modifications, but does not conform to the modifications made under this provision.

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70204, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Trump accounts and contribution pilot program
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
72, 128, 139J, 219, 408, 529A, 530A, 6213, 6434, 6659, 6693, conforming amendment to 4973
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17131,17140.4, 18631, 19051, 23711.4
Summary of Federal Change

This provision creates an individual retirement account, also known as a “Trump account”. A “Trump account” is defined as an individual retirement account (IRA) under IRC section 408(a) that is not designated as a Roth IRA and is for the benefit of an eligible individual or their beneficiaries. This provision defines an “eligible individual” as an individual (beneficiary) who has not turned 18 years before the end of the calendar year and who has a valid social security number (SSN). The account must be invested in an established mutual fund or stock exchange fund.

This provision does not allow a deduction for contributions made to the Trump Account before the first day of the calendar year that the eligible individual attains age 18. Contributions are limited to $5,000 per calendar year until the calendar year that the eligible individual turns 18 and a cost-of-living adjustment will be applied to that amount beginning after 2027. If the eligible individual dies before their 18th birthday, the account ceases to be a Trump Account and any person or estate of the beneficiary who acquires the account must include in their gross income the fair market value of the account assets (reduced by the investment in the contract) in the year of the death of the account beneficiary.

Distributions are allowed from Trump Accounts beginning January 1 of the calendar year that the individual turns 18 years old. Excess contributions to the account can be distributed before the eligible individual turns 18, are not included in the gross income of the eligible individual and that amount of net income that is attributable to the excess contribution is subject to 100 percent tax. Any withdrawals for nonqualified expenses are treated as ordinary income and subject to the income tax rate and a 10 percent early withdrawal penalty if distributions are taken before the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 18 years old and not used for rollovers to qualified ABLE rollover contributions or a rollover of the entire balance of the account to another Trump Account for that same beneficiary.

This provision also allows an employer to make contributions, limited to $2,500, adjusted annually for inflation, per calendar year, on behalf of their employee who establishes an account on behalf of an eligible individual. These accounts are not treated as a simplified employee retirement account or SIMPLE account by the employer. The employer’s contribution amount is excluded from the employee’s gross income.

Contributions can also be made by tax-exempt organizations to an eligible individual’s account or account established for a qualified class of eligible individuals as general funding contributions, as defined. These contributions would not count toward the $5,000 contribution limit.

This provision also creates a pilot program where the federal government will deposit $1,000 into a Trump Account for those that make this election for eligible children born after December 31, 2024, and before January 1, 2029. These contributions would not count toward the $5,000 contribution limit. The $1,000 payment would not be subject to reduction or offset for past due support under the Social Security Act, debts owed to federal agencies, state income tax obligations, unemployment compensation debts, or assessed federal taxes subject to levy or collection. The eligible child must be a U.S. citizen and have an SSN. This provision will impose a penalty of $500 or $1,000, respectively, if the account is negligently or fraudulently established. An omission of the correct SSN on the return for the child, or taxpayer claiming the child, or taxpayer’s spouse, is treated as a math or clerical error.

California Impact

Under RTC sections 17501 and 24601, California automatically conforms to the federal changes made to Part I of Subchapter D of Chapter 1 of Subtitle A of the Internal Revenue Code, which includes IRC sections 402, 408, and 408A. However, California does not automatically conform to the Trump Account provisions under IRC section 530A that was added under Subchapter F.

California conforms, under the PITL, relating to items that are specifically excluded from gross income in RTC section 17131, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025. The federal $1,000 pilot contributions to Trump Accounts for children born in 2025 through 2028 are treated as a payment against the federal tax and provides a refund of that payment to the eligible child's Trump Account under IRC section 6434. California does not conform to IRC section 6434. However, under California's conformity to IRC section 61, the $1000 contribution would not be considered income.

Under the specified date of January 1, 2025, California does not conform to the exclusion for certain employer contributions to a Trump account.

Under the Administration of Franchise and Income Tax Law (AFITL), Franchise Tax Board treats specified errors identified on the return during processing as math errors, which includes not providing a valid identification number as required to claim a dependent exemption tax credit, earned income tax credit, young child tax credit, or foster youth tax credit. California does not conform to the definition of mathematical or clerical error under IRC section 6213. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision related to IRC section 6213.

California does not conform to the provision's penalty for a negligent or fraudulent election.

Revenue Impact

The estimated revenue impact to conform to the above federal provisions would result in the following loss:

26/27 27/28 28/29 29/30
($1,000,000) ($900,000) ($1,600,000) ($3,000,000)

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70301, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Full expensing for certain business property
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Generally, operative for property acquired after 01/19/2025. Applies to certain plants bearing fruits and nuts planted or grafted after 01/19/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
168, conforming changes to 460
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17201, 17250, 24349
Summary of Federal Change

The provision makes several changes to the additional first year (bonus) depreciation for qualified property, previously established under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 13201), as follows:

  • Makes permanent the 100 percent additional first year depreciation for qualified property acquired after January 19, 2025.
  • Adds “qualified sound recording production” as qualified property eligible for bonus depreciation.
  • Removes self-constructed property from the special rules relating to bonus depreciation.
  • Modifies the special rule relating to certain plants bearing fruits and nuts which are planted or grafted by removing the operative date of January 1, 2027, and allowing the 100 percent additional bonus depreciation.
  • Repeals the phase down percentages.
  • Allows qualified property placed in service and specified plants planted and grafted during the first taxable year ending after January 19, 2025, to transition from specified phase down percentages to 100 percent if elected by the taxpayer.
California Impact

California conforms, under the PITL, to the federal rules relating to MACRS depreciation, under IRC section 168, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications. However, the PITL specifically does not conform to bonus depreciation; thus, the provision that modifies and extends bonus depreciation is not applicable under the PITL.

California does not conform, under the CTL, to IRC section 168, relating to MACRS depreciation. The CTL is in substantial conformity to the pre-1981 Class Life Asset Depreciation Range System (ADR) deductions. The ADR is an accounting method established by the IRS based on the “useful life” of depreciable property.

The CTL allows “additional first-year depreciation” of up to $10,000 per year. However, the CTL allows taxpayers to elect the IRC section 179 expensing deduction in lieu of “additional first-year depreciation.” Property qualifying for “additional first-year depreciation” is similar to property qualifying under IRC section 179. However, a corporation is allowed only one or the other of the expensing deductions, not both.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70302, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Full expensing of domestic research and experimental expenditures
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Generally, applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2024. At the election of eligible taxpayers for domestic expenditures paid or incurred for taxable years beginning after 12/31/2021 and before 01/01/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
174A, 174, 280C; conforming changes to 41, 56, 59, 144, 195, 263, 543, 864, 1016, 1202; and uncodified sections affecting IRC section 481
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17201, 17201.1, 17270, 23051.5, 24365, 24440
Summary of Federal Change

This provision creates a new IRC section 174A to allow a deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures in the year paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024. The provision defines the term “domestic research or experimental expenditures” as research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred by the taxpayer in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business other than expenditures that are attributable to qualified foreign research activities under the federal research credit as defined in IRC section 41(d)(4)(F).

This provision allows a taxpayer to charge domestic research and experimental expenditures to a capital account and amortize those expenditures ratably over 60 months. The taxpayer may also elect to take the deduction on a prior timely filed return, which would be after December 31, 2021.

This provision would apply the following special rules:

  • Expenditures for the acquisition or improvement of land or improvement of property used in connection with research or experimentation that is depreciated would not be allowed to apply the deduction.
  • Expenditures paid or incurred to determine the existence of, location, extent or quality of ore deposits, or other mineral including oil and gas, would not be allowed to apply the deduction.
  • Amounts paid or incurred for the development of software can be treated as a research or experimental expenditure.

The provision modifies IRC section 174 and replaces the term “specified” with “foreign” to identify research or experimental expenditures. Foreign research or experimental expenditures are required to be amortized ratably over the 15-year period. The definition of foreign research or experimental expenditures is modified to include expenditures which are attributable to qualified foreign research activities under the federal research credit (as defined in IRC section 41(d)(4)(F)).

Additionally, the research credit is amended to add the deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures (IRC section 174A).

The provision amends IRC section 280(c)(1) to require taxpayers to reduce the deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC section 174A by the amount of the research credit allowed under IRC section 41. Deductions for domestic and foreign research or experimental expenditures are also required to be calculated when computing alternative minimum tax under IRC section 56(b)(2).

The provisions and treatment, as described above, related to IRC section 174A, are treated as a change in method of accounting for purposes of IRC section 481.

California Impact

California does not conform to IRC 174A. California conforms, under the PITL and the CTL, to IRC section 174, relating to research and experimental expenditures, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, but does not conform to the modification to the federal changes relating to the deduction of research and experimental expenditures.

Additionally, California generally conforms, under the PITL and the CTL, to IRC section 280C, relating to the credit for increasing research activities, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025. However, California does not conform to the federal changes that require the deduction of domestic research or experimental expenditures be reduced by the amount of research credit allowed.

Revenue Impact

The estimated revenue impact to conform to the above federal provisions would result in the following loss:

Negligible Negligible Negligible Negligible

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Extension and enhancement of paid family and medical leave credit
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025

Taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
45S and conforming changes to 280C
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
N/A
Summary of Federal Change

The provision makes permanent the employer credit for paid family and medical leave created under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 13403).

The provision also expands the eligibility for employers to claim a general business credit for paid family and medical leave to include premiums paid or incurred for an insurance policy, regardless of whether any qualifying employees were on family and medical leave during the taxable year. The provision would allow any leave paid by State or local government to be taken into account when determining the amount of family and medical leave provided by the employer but that leave should not be used when determining the amount of credit. Additionally, there cannot be a double benefit for the premiums paid or incurred as a deduction as provided in IRC section 280C.

The provision also modifies the definition of “qualifying employee” to require that the employee be customarily employed for not less than 20 hours per week and, at the election of the employer, must be employed for not less than six months. The definition also specifies that compensation be determined on an annualized basis, or pro-rata for part-time employees.

The provision also modifies the “aggregation rules” to provide that all persons treated as a single employer under IRC section 414 are treated as a single employer unless the person has a substantial and legitimate business reason for not having a written family medical leave policy as specified.

California Impact

California does not conform to IRC section 45S, relating to the employer credit for paid family and medical leave, and has no comparable credit. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Special depreciation allowance for qualified production property

07/04/2025

Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
168, 1245
California Conforms?

Relevant RTC Sections
17201, 17250, 17859, 18151, 24349
Summary of Federal Change

The provision classifies and adds “any qualified production property” as property that is depreciated under modified accelerated cost recovery system (MACRS). However, the provision allows a taxpayer a special depreciation deduction of 100 percent of the adjusted basis for any qualified production property placed in service during the taxable year and the adjusted basis must be reduced by the amount of the deduction before computing the allowable depreciation deduction. The provision defines qualified production property as the portion of any nonresidential real property that meets the following:

  • Used as an integral part of the qualified production activity
    • However, qualified property where the taxpayer is a lessor and the property is used by a lessee cannot be considered to be used by the taxpayer as part of a qualified production activity.
  • Placed in service in the United States or any possession of the United States
  • Original use commences with the taxpayer
  • Construction begins after January 19, 2025, and before January 1, 2029
  • Designated by the taxpayer as an election under this provision, and
  • Placed in service before January 1, 2031.

The provision excludes from qualified production property a portion of any nonresidential real property which is used for office space, administrative services, lodging, parking, sales activities, research, software or engineering, or other functions unrelated to the manufacturing, production, or refining of tangible personal property.

The provision includes special rules to allow the deduction for property acquired by the taxpayer after January 19, 2025, and before January 1, 2029, and if the property was not previously used in qualified production activities during the period beginning on January 1, 2021, and ending on May 12,2025. Additionally, the provision defines qualified production activity to include the manufacturing, production, or refining of a qualified product. Production includes only agricultural and chemical production. The provision also defines a qualified product as any tangible personal property if such property is not a food or beverage that is prepared in the same building as a retail establishment in which such property is sold.

The provision also allows the Secretary to determine an extension for the placed in-service date, if the Secretary determines that an act of God prevents the taxpayer from placing such property in service before such date. This provision allows special depreciation allowances for qualified production property and does not include property where the alternative depreciation system applies.

The provision requires recapture under IRC section 1245 of any qualified production property if within 10 years of the date the property is placed in service, the property ceases to be used as qualified production property, and how the property is used changes.

California Impact

California conforms with modifications, under the PITL, to the federal rules relating to MACRS depreciation, under IRC section 168, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025. However, California does not conform to this provision to allow the special depreciation treatment for any qualified production property.

California also conforms with modification, under the PITL, to the federal rules relating to capital gains and losses, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, but does not conform to treatment of any qualified production property as IRC section 1245 property.

California does not conform, under the CTL, to IRC section 168, relating to MACRS depreciation. The CTL is in substantial conformity to the pre-1981 Class Life Asset Depreciation Range System (ADR) deductions. The ADR is an accounting method established by the IRS based on the “useful life” of depreciable property.

Revenue Impact

Title

One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Summary of Federal Change

This provision modifies the computation of taxable income for purposes of calculating the foreign tax credit (FTC) limitation (Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 904(b)) on net controlled foreign corporation (CFC) tested income, other than passive category income, included in a United States (U.S.) shareholder’s gross income for the taxable year (IRC section 904(d)(1)(A)). For purposes of this provision, a U.S. shareholder of any CFC is required to include in their gross income their share of net CFC tested income for the taxable year (IRC section 951A). Net CFC tested income is the U.S. shareholders excess (if any) of their aggregate pro rata share of CFC tested income for the taxable year, over the U.S shareholders CFC tested loss for the taxable year (IRC section 951A(b)).

This provision requires a U.S. shareholder to allocate and apportion certain deductions to foreign sourced net CFC tested income, except for interest expense and research and experimental expenditures. These deductions include any deduction allowed under the foreign derived deduction eligible income on net CFC tested income (IRC section 250(a)(1)(B)), state and local, foreign, income, war profits, and excess profits taxes (IRC section 164(a)(3)) or any other deduction directly allocable to their share of foreign sourced income.

This provision also amends IRC sections 904 and 951A related to the treatment of certain categories of foreign sourced income.

California does not allow a FTC and does not conform to subpart F (sections 951 to 965) of the IRC, relating to CFCs, except to the extent applicable with respect to filings under a water’s-edge election. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

This provision increases the percentage of foreign income taxes deemed paid for taxes properly attributable to net CFC tested income. Net CFC tested income is the United States (U.S.) shareholder’s excess (if any) of their aggregate pro rata share of CFC tested income for the taxable year, over the U.S. shareholder’s CFC tested loss for the taxable year (IRC section 951A(b)). The provision increases the percentage of foreign income taxes deemed-paid from 80 percent to 90 percent of the product of the domestic corporation’s Section 951A percentage inclusion by the aggregate tested foreign income taxes paid or accrued by the CFC.

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70313, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Sourcing certain income from the sale of inventory produced in the United States
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
904
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17024.5, 17951, 23040.1, 23051.5, 25110
Summary of Federal Change

The provision modifies the taxable income computation for the purposes of calculating the FTC limitation (Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 904(b)) on sourcing of certain inventory produced in the United States (U.S.) and sold through foreign branches. For the purpose of this provision, if a U.S. person maintains an office or other fixed place of business in a foreign country, as determined under IRC section 864(c)(5), the portion of income from a sale or exchange outside the U.S. of inventory property that is produced in the U.S., used outside of the U.S., and derived from the purchase of inventory property within a possession of the U.S, and is attributable to that office or fixed place of business, is treated as foreign source income. The amount treated as foreign source income under this provision may not exceed 50 percent of the income from the sale or exchange of such property.

California Impact

California does not conform to the sourcing rules under IRC sections 861 to 865. California exercises its taxing powers based on two jurisdictional concepts: (1) the residency of the individual, and (2) the source of the income. Residents of California pay state taxes on all income received regardless of its geographical source. Nonresidents of California are taxed by California only on income derived from sources within California’s boundaries (“source income”). Source income includes wages earned from services performed in California, gains from the disposition of property located in California, and profits from business transacted in California. Intangible income, such as investment interest, is considered to originate in the state in which the recipient resides at the time it is earned, unless it is earned in connection with a trade or business.

California does not allow a FTC and does not conform to subpart F (sections 951 to 965) of the IRC, relating to controlled foreign corporations, except to the extent applicable with respect to filings under a water’s-edge election.

As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70321, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Modification of deduction for foreign-derived deduction eligible income and net CFC tested income
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
250
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
24411, 25106, 25110
Summary of Federal Change

The provision modifies the deduction from gross income allowed to a domestic corporation for foreign-derived deduction eligible income, which is calculated as an amount equal to the sum of a percentage of the foreign-derived deduction eligible income of a domestic corporation in a taxable year plus a percentage of the net controlled foreign corporation (CFC) tested income included in gross income of that domestic corporation under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 951A for the taxable year and the gross-up amount treated as a dividend received under IRC section 78 for that domestic corporation for the taxable year. The provision decreases both percentages: 37.5 percent to 33.34 percent for the foreign-derived deduction eligible income and 50 percent to 40 percent for the net CFC tested income included in gross income under IRC section 951A and the gross-up amount treated as a dividend received under IRC section 78 for the taxable year. The overall impact would decrease the deduction amount allowed for taxable years beginning on or after December 31, 2025.

California Impact

California does not conform to the changes to IRC section 250.

Worldwide Unitary Method

California corporate taxpayers doing business both within and without California are required to compute their California franchise or income tax using the worldwide unitary method. Under this method, a corporate taxpayer's business income from both domestic and foreign unitary operations is considered in the calculation of the taxpayer's tax base, and a share of that business income is then “apportioned” to California using a formula. Income apportioned to California is subject to California franchise or income tax. The formula measures relative levels of business activity in the state by using the amount of the taxpayer’s sales in California divided by the taxpayer's sales everywhere. This measure of activities is commonly called the “single sales-factor formula.” The amount of sales from both domestic and foreign activities are included in the calculation of the apportionment formula. Generally, dividends paid from one member to another within the unitary group from unitary earnings are eliminated from tax computations under Revenue and Taxation Code (RTC) section 25106.

California Water's-Edge Election

As an alternative to the worldwide unitary method, California law allows corporations to elect to determine the business income of their combined reporting group on a “water's-edge” basis. In general, the water’s-edge method excludes foreign corporations from the calculation of business income. An exception to this general rule is a CFC with subpart F income. The income and factors of the CFC are included in a water's-edge combined report based on the CFC's inclusion ratio. This ratio is equal to the CFC’s current year subpart F income divided by the CFC’s current year earnings and profits. While California does not conform to the subpart F scheme of the IRC, for purposes of computing the CFC's inclusion ratio under water's-edge, California incorporates the federal definitions of "subpart F income" and "earnings and profits" as applicable for federal income tax purposes for the same taxable year.

Generally, rather than computing a dividends-received deduction using federal dividends received deduction (DRD) provisions, dividends paid to the water's-edge combined reporting group from foreign affiliates are income on the water's-edge combined report and California taxpayers electing water's-edge treatment are generally entitled to a 75 percent DRD on such dividends under RTC section 24411.

As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Summary of Federal Change

An applicable taxpayer is required to pay a tax equal to the Base Erosion Minimum Tax (BEMT) amount for the taxable year. Under this provision, the BEMT amount is the excess of 10.5 percent of the modified taxable income of the taxpayer for the taxable year over an amount equal to the regular tax liability (defined in Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 26(b)) of the taxpayer for the taxable year reduced (but not below zero) by the excess (if any) of the credits allowed under Chapter 1 against such regular tax liability over the sum of: (1) the credit allowed under IRC section 38 for the taxable year which is properly allocable to the research credit determined under IRC section 41(a), plus (2) the portion of the applicable IRC section 38 credits not in excess of 80 percent of the lesser of the amount of such credits or the BEMT amount (determined without regard to this clause).

This provision repeals the modifications established under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 14401), including repealing the increase in the percentage of modified taxable income used to calculate the BEMT from 10 percent to 12.5 percent and instead replaced 10 percent with 10.5 percent, redesigned several subsections and made other technical changes to conform to the amendments under this section.

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70341, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Coordination of business interest limitation with interest capitalization provisions
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
163
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17201, 24344
Summary of Federal Change

This provision would require taxpayers to calculate their business interest deduction limitation on (1) business interest income; (2) 30 percent of the adjusted taxable income of the taxpayer for the taxable year; and (3) the floor plan financing interest of the taxpayer for the taxable year (Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 163(j), regardless of whether the taxpayer deducts or capitalizes such business interest. In addition, the provision provides that the amount of allowable business interest deduction would be applied first to the aggregate amount to business interest that would otherwise be capitalized, and the remainder (if any) would be applied to the aggregate amount of business interest that would be deducted.

In general, any carryforward business interest allowed under this provision would not be treated as interest to which an interest capitalization provision applies. This provision adds and defines the term “interest capitalization provision” to mean any interest that is required to be charged to a capital account or may be deducted or charged to a capital account.

This provision also modifies the definition of “business interest,” for purposes of calculating the business interest limitation, to mean any interest paid or accrued on indebtedness properly allocable to a trade or business, except for investment interest or any capitalized interest. For purposes of this provision, “investment interest” is defined as any interest paid or accrued allowed as a deduction on indebtedness properly allocable to property held for investment (IRC section 163(d)). Capitalized interest includes (1) interest and carrying charges properly allocable to personal property which is part of a straddle (IRC section 263(g)) or (2) interest paid or incurred during a production period for real or tangible property produced by a taxpayer that has a long useful life, an estimated production period exceeding 2 years, or an estimated production period exceeding 1 year and estimated cost of $1,000,000 (IRC section 263A(f)).

The provision also provides that the Secretary will issue regulations or guidance as may be necessary to carry out the purpose of these provisions, including regulations or guidance to determine which business interest will be taken into account for purposes of these provisions and when determining which portion of the deduction will be allocated to related and nonrelated parties (IRC section 59A(c)(3)).

California Impact

California conforms, under the Personal Income Tax Law to the federal rules for the deduction of interest under IRC section 163, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision under the PITL.

Under the Corporation Tax Law (CTL), to the federal rules for the deduction of interest under IRC section 163, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications, but does not conform to the federal limitations on deductions of business interest . As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision under the CTL.
