Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70353, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Restoration of limitation on downward attribution of stock ownership in applying constructive ownership rules
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to taxable years of foreign corporations beginning after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
951B, 958
California Conforms?
Partially
Relevant RTC Sections
25110
Summary of Federal Change

Federal law provides rules to determine stock ownership of a corporation, including requirements for direct ownership, indirect ownership, and constructive ownership, to determine whether a foreign corporation is a foreign owned controlled foreign corporation (CFC) and for purposes of determining the amounts includable in a United States (U.S.) shareholder’s gross income from a foreign owned CFC.

Prior to the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) (Public Law (P.L.) 115-97), for purposes of determining constructive ownership, federal law prohibited downward attribution, meaning that certain stock of a foreign corporation owned by a foreign person was not attributed to a related U.S. person for purposes of determining whether the related U.S. person was a U.S. shareholder of the foreign corporation and whether the foreign corporation was a CFC. In 2017, the TCJA (P.L. 115-97, section 14213) amended the constructive ownership rules of Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 958(b) to repeal that prohibition on downward attribution.

This provision amends the ownership attribution rules of IRC section 958(b) to restore the prohibition on downward attribution of stock ownership of IRC section 958(b)(4) that was repealed by the TCJA (P.L. 115-97, section 14213). It also adds to subpart F, IRC section 951B, the income inclusion rules that would be applied with respect to such U.S. shareholders of a foreign owned CFC.

In addition, the provision defines a “foreign controlled United States shareholder” with respect to any foreign corporation, if a U.S. shareholder with respect to such foreign corporation (1) owns 50 percent or more of the foreign corporation, and (2) the IRC section 958(b) constructive ownership rules were applied without regard to IRC section 318(a)(3)(A),(B), and (C) that apply to a person who is not a U.S. person.

The provision also defines “foreign controlled foreign corporation” as a foreign corporation, other than a CFC, which would be a CFC if the CFC definition of IRC section 957(a) was satisfied with ownership of “foreign controlled United States shareholders,” rather than “United States shareholders."

California Impact

California conforms to the changes to IRC section 958, but does not conform to the changes to IRC section 951B.

Worldwide Unitary Method

California corporate taxpayers doing business both within and without California are required to compute their California franchise or income tax using the worldwide unitary method. Under this method, a corporate taxpayer's business income from both domestic and foreign unitary operations is considered in the calculation of the taxpayer's tax base, and a share of that business income is then “apportioned” to California using a formula. Income apportioned to California is subject to California franchise or income tax. The formula measures relative levels of business activity in the state by using the amount of the taxpayer’s sales in California divided by the taxpayer's sales everywhere. This measure of activities is commonly called the “single sales-factor formula.” The amount of sales from both domestic and foreign activities are included in the calculation of the apportionment formula. Generally, dividends paid from one member to another within the unitary group from unitary earnings are eliminated from tax computations under Revenue and Taxation Code (RTC) section 25106.

California Water's-Edge Election

As an alternative to the worldwide unitary method, California law allows corporations to elect to determine the business income of their combined reporting group on a “water's-edge” basis. In general, the water’s-edge method excludes foreign corporations from the calculation of business income. An exception to this general rule is a CFC with subpart F income. The income and factors of the CFC are included in a water's-edge combined report based on the CFC's inclusion ratio. This ratio is equal to the CFC’s current year subpart F income divided by the CFC’s current year earnings and profits.

While California does not conform to the subpart F scheme of the IRC, for purposes of computing the CFC's inclusion ratio under water's-edge, California incorporates the federal definitions of a “controlled foreign corporation,” “subpart F income” and “earnings and profits ” as applicable for federal income tax purposes for the same taxable year. This is limited to provisions of the IRC referred to in the water's-edge election provisions that are not otherwise applicable for California franchise or income tax purposes.

RTC section 25110 specifically refers to ""controlled foreign corporation"" as defined in IRC section 957. IRC section 957 applies the stock ownership rules under IRC section 958 to determine if a foreign corporation meets the U.S. shareholder ownership requirement to be a controlled foreign corporation. As a result, the new ownership attribution rule is applicable with respect to water's-edge elections for taxable years of foreign corporations beginning after December 31, 2025, and for taxable years of U.S. shareholders in which or within which such taxable years of foreign corporations end.

California does not conform to the provisions of Section 951B.

Revenue Impact
26/27 27/28 28/29 29/30
Baseline Baseline Baseline Baseline

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70354, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Modifications to pro rata share rules
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
The provision applies to taxable years of foreign corporations beginning after 12/31/2025. Additionally, a transition rule for dividends provides that a dividend paid (or deemed paid) by a controlled foreign corporation (CFC) shall not be treated as a dividend for purposes of applying section 951 provided the dividend was paid (or deemed paid) on or before 06/28/2025, during the taxable year of such CFC which includes such date and the United States (U.S.) shareholder did not own the stock of such CFC during the portion of such taxable year on or before 06/28/2025, or was paid (or deemed paid) after 06/28/2025, and before such CFC’s first taxable year beginning after 12/31/2025, and such dividend does not increase the taxable income of a U.S. person that is subject to federal income tax for the taxable year.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
951, with conforming amendments to 951A, 956
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
25110
Summary of Federal Change

Federal law provides income reporting rules for U.S. shareholders of a CFC. This provision provides that if a foreign corporation is a CFC at any time during the taxable year, each U.S. shareholder that owns stock in such corporation on any day during the CFC taxable year, is required to include in the U.S. shareholder’s gross income its pro rata share of the corporation’s subpart F income for the CFC’s taxable year as determined by the portion of such income that is attributable to the stock of such corporation owned by the shareholder and any period of the CFC year during which the shareholder owned the stock, such shareholder was a U.S. shareholder, and such corporation was a CFC. Each U.S. shareholder that owns stock in such corporation on the last day of the CFC taxable year, is required to include in the U.S. shareholder’s gross income its pro rata share of any amount as determined under IRC section 956 with respect to investment of earnings in U.S. property.

This provision also provides that any amount required to be included in gross income by a U.S. shareholder shall be included in gross income for the U.S. shareholder’s taxable year that includes the last day on which the shareholder owns (within the meaning of IRC section 958(a)) stock in the CFC during such CFC taxable year.

California Impact

California does not conform to the changes to IRC sections 951, 951A, or 956.

Worldwide Unitary Method

California corporate taxpayers doing business both within and without California are required to compute their California franchise or income tax using the worldwide unitary method. Under this method, a corporate taxpayer's business income from both domestic and foreign unitary operations is considered in the calculation of the taxpayer's tax base, and a share of that business income is then “apportioned” to California using a formula. Income apportioned to California is subject to California franchise or income tax. The formula measures relative levels of business activity in the state by using the amount of the taxpayer’s sales in California divided by the taxpayer's sales everywhere. This measure of activities is commonly called the “single sales-factor formula.” The amount of sales from both domestic and foreign activities are included in the calculation of the apportionment formula. Generally, dividends paid from one member to another within the unitary group from unitary earnings are eliminated from tax computations under Revenue and Taxation Code (RTC) section 25106.

California Water's-Edge Election

As an alternative to the worldwide unitary method, California law allows corporations to elect to determine the business income of their combined reporting group on a “water's-edge” basis. In general, the water’s-edge method excludes foreign corporations from the calculation of business income. An exception to this general rule is a CFC with subpart F income. The income and factors of the CFC are included in a water's-edge combined report based on the CFC's inclusion ratio. This ratio is equal to the CFC’s current year subpart F income divided by the CFC’s current year earnings and profits. While California does not conform to the subpart F scheme of the IRC, for purposes of computing the CFC's inclusion ratio under water's-edge, California incorporates the federal definitions of "subpart F income" and "earnings and profits" as applicable for federal income tax purposes for the same taxable year.

Generally, rather than computing a dividends-received deduction using federal dividends received deduction (DRD) provisions, dividends paid to the water's-edge combined reporting group from foreign affiliates are income on the water's-edge combined report and California taxpayers electing water's-edge treatment are generally entitled to a 75 percent DRD on such dividends under RTC section 24411.

In addition, California does not conform to IRC section 956 with respect to investment of earnings in U.S. property.

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70401, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Enhancement of employer-provided child care credit
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to amounts paid or incurred after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
45F
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
N/A
Summary of Federal Change

This provision modifies the employer-provided child care credit by increasing the percentage of qualified child care expenditures eligible for the credit from 25 percent to 40 percent. For eligible small businesses, the percentage of qualified child care expenditures is increased to 50 percent.

The provision increases the maximum credit amount to $500,000 and in the case of an eligible small business, the limit is increased to $600,000; these limits would be adjusted for inflation annually for taxable years beginning after 2026. Beginning after 2026, the credit amounts of $500,000 and $600,000, would be adjusted using a cost-of-living calculation.

This provision expands the definition of “eligible small business” to include a business that meets the gross receipts test under IRC section 448(c), meaning that the average annual gross receipts for the partnership or corporation do not exceed $25,000,000, adjusted for inflation after 2018. The adjusted amount for 2025 was $31,000,000. This provision, for purposes of this credit, modifies the gross receipts test to include the previous five-taxable-year period, instead of three taxable year.

This provision expands qualified child care expenditures allowed under a contract with a qualified child care facility to also include contracts with an intermediate entity that contracts with one or more qualified child care facilities to provide child care services. Additionally, this provision expands eligible child care facilities to include facilities that are jointly owned or operated. The Secretary of the Treasury is required to issue regulations or other guidance that may be necessary to carry out these two amendments to the credit.

California Impact

California does not conform to the employer-provided child care credit.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70402, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Enhancement of adoption credit
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2024.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
23
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17052.25
Summary of Federal Change

The provision modifies the adoption credit by allowing refundability of up to $5,000 of allowable adoption expenses paid or incurred by the taxpayer and excludes refunded adoption credits from credit amounts eligible to be carried forward for use in succeeding taxable years.

This provision provides that the credit amount eligible for refundability would be adjusted annually for inflation.

California Impact

California does not conform to IRC section 23, relating to adoption expenses.

California has a standalone adoption credit, which allows a credit equal to 50 percent (not to exceed $2,500) of the cost of adopting a minor child who is an American citizen and is in the custody of a California public agency or a political subdivision of California. The credit is claimed in the taxable year in which the decree or order of adoption is entered, although qualifying costs paid or incurred in prior years can qualify for the credit.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70405, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Enhancement of child and dependent care tax credit
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
21
California Conforms?
Yes, with modifications
Relevant RTC Sections
17052.6
Summary of Federal Change

The child and dependent care credit is for employment-related expenses paid during a taxable year, calculated as a percentage of eligible expenses that are limited to $3,000 for 1 qualifying individual and $6,000 for 2 or more qualifying individuals.

This provision increases the applicable percentage for employment-related expenses from 35 percent to 50 percent. The provision also modifies the two-part phase out applicable to the 50 percent credit rate. Under the first part, the 50 percent credit rate is reduced, but not below 35 percent, by 1 percentage point for each $2,000, or fraction thereof, of adjusted gross income (AGI) above $15,000. Under the second part, the 35 percent credit rate "floor" is reduced, but not below 20 percent, by 1 percentage point for each $2,000 ($4,000 in the case of a joint return), or fraction thereof, of AGI above $75,000 ($150,000 in the case of a joint return).

California Impact

California automatically conforms to the child and dependent care credit, with modifications and these changes impact the computation of the California credit.

The California child and dependent care credit is allowed based on a percentage of the taxpayer’s federal child and dependent care tax credit for the taxable year. The percentages are:

Credit percentage Credit percentage
$40,000 50%
Over $40,000 but not over $70,000 43%
Over $70,000 but not over $100,000 34%
Over $100,000 0%

The credit is limited to household services and care provided within California.

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70411, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Tax credit for contributions of individuals to scholarship granting organizations
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
The credit provision applies to taxable years ending after 12/31/2026. The gross income exclusion applies to amounts received after 12/31/2026, in taxable years ending after such date.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
25F, 139K
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17131
Summary of Federal Change

The provision provides an income tax credit, limited to $1,700 per taxable year, to individual taxpayers that make a charitable cash contribution to an eligible organization that uses the contributions to grant scholarships for eligible students. The credit is required to be reduced by any amount allowed as a state tax credit for contributions made by the taxpayer during the taxable year. Additionally, any contributions for which the new credit is allowed is not considered for purposes of calculating the taxpayer’s charitable contribution deduction. The credit may be carried over for a maximum of five taxable years.

The provision requires an eligible, tax-exempt scholarship granting organization to (1) provide scholarships to 10 or more students who do not all attend the same school, (2) use 90 percent of the organization’s income on scholarships, (3) limit grants to qualified elementary or secondary education expenses, and (4) provide preference to prior year recipients and recipients with siblings, among additional requirements.

A student, scholarship recipient, must be eligible to enroll in a public elementary or secondary school and report prior year household income not to exceed 300 percent of the area median gross income.

The provision provides a gross income exclusion to the individual or dependent of that individual for scholarships received for qualified elementary or secondary education expenses of an eligible student, provided by a scholarship granting organization.

California Impact

California does not conform to the tax credit for contributions to scholarship granting organizations.

California conforms by reference to Part III of Subchapter B of Chapter 1 of Subtitle A of the IRC, relating to items that are specifically excluded from gross income, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, in RTC section 17131. As a result, California does not conform to the gross income exclusion for scholarships for qualified elementary or secondary education expenses.

Revenue Impact

The estimated revenue impact to conform to the above provision would result in the following loss:

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70412, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Exclusion for employer payments of student loans
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to payments made after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
127
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17131, 17151, 17154
Summary of Federal Change

This provision permanently enables employers to provide a student loan repayment benefit to employees on a tax-free basis. The repayment benefit was temporary under the Coronavirus, Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act (CARES Act) (Public Law (P.L.) 116-136, section 2206) for payments made after March 27, 2020 and before January 1, 2021, and the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 (P.L. 116-260, section 120) extended the provision through 2025.

This provision makes the exclusion permanent, applicable to payments made by an employer on behalf of an employee after December 31, 2025. Under the provision, an employer may contribute up to $5,250 annually toward payment of an employee’s student loans, and such contribution would be excluded from the employee’s income. The $5,250 cap applies to both the student loan repayment benefit as well as other educational assistance (e.g., tuition, fees, books) provided by the employer.

Additionally, beginning in taxable year 2025, the provision provides an inflation, cost-of-living adjustment for the $5,250 income exclusion cap.

California Impact

California does not conform to federal rules relating to educational assistance programs under IRC section 127, but has stand-alone language in RTC section 17151 that allows for an exclusion from gross income of an employee for amounts paid or incurred by their employer, not to exceed $5,250, for education assistance pursuant to an educational assistance program, similar to IRC section 127. As a result, California does not conform to IRC section 127 federal exclusion for certain employer educational assistance, including payments of student loans, or the inflation adjustment to the income exclusion cap.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70413, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Additional expenses treated as qualified higher education expenses for purposes of 529 accounts
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to distributions for eligible elementary and secondary tuition qualified higher education expenses made after 07/04/2025. The provision that modifies the qualified higher education expense limit, applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
529
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17140, 17140.3, 23711, 23711.5, 24306
Summary of Federal Change

The provision expands the type of expenses eligible for an IRC section 529 distribution. Under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 11032), a distribution was previously limited to tuition expenses in connection with the enrollment or attendance of the designated beneficiary at a public, private, or religious elementary or secondary school. Under the provision, in addition to tuition expenses, qualified higher education expenses, for an elementary or secondary private, public, or religious school, also includes expenses for curriculum and curricular materials, books or other instruction materials, online educational materials, tuition for specified tutoring or educational classes, fees for specified examinations, fees for dual enrollment in an institution of higher education, and specified educational therapies for students with disabilities.

The provision increases the IRC section 529 plan distribution limit from $10,000 to $20,000, for eligible expenses incurred during the taxable year in connection with the enrollment or attendance of the designated beneficiary at a public, private or religious elementary or secondary school. This limitation applies on a per-student basis, rather than a per-account basis.

California Impact

California law, under the PITL and the CTL, conforms to IRC section 529, relating to qualified tuition programs, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications, and does not conform to IRC section 529 account funding for elementary and secondary education. As a result, CA does not conform to the provision’s new federal rules relating to expanded qualified expenses or to the increased maximum distribution amount.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70414, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Certain postsecondary credentialing expenses treated as qualified higher education expenses for purposes of 529 accounts
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Applies to distributions made after 07/04/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
529
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17140, 17140.3, 23711, 23711.5, 24306
Summary of Federal Change

The provision provides that qualified postsecondary credentialing expenses are to be treated as qualified higher education expenses eligible for an IRC section 529 distribution. The provision defines eligible postsecondary credentialing expenses to include tuition, fees, books, supplies, and equipment required for enrollment or attendance at a recognized, postsecondary credential program, and any other expense incurred in connection with enrollment or attendance at a recognized postsecondary credential program if the expense would be considered a higher education expense if incurred in connection with enrollment or attendance at an eligible education institution. Qualified postsecondary credentialing expenses also include fees for testing if it is required to obtain or maintain a recognized postsecondary credential, and fees for continuing education is required to maintain a recognized postsecondary credential.

Recognized postsecondary credential means a credential that is issued by a program accredited by the Institute for Credentialing Excellence, the National Commission on Certifying Agencies, or the American National Standards Institute, as well as any program included in the Credentialing Opportunities On-Line directory maintained by the Department of Defense or any branch of the Armed Forces, or programs identified by the Secretary.

California Impact

California law, under the PITL and the CTL, conforms to IRC section 529, relating to qualified tuition programs, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications, and does not conform to IRC section 529 rules relating to postsecondary credentialing expenses. As a result, CA does not conform to the provision’s new federal rules for treating postsecondary credentialing expenses as qualified higher education expenses.

The California Kids Investment and Development Savings Program (CalKIDS), administered by the Scholarshare Investment Board, authorizes low-income individuals to establish accounts in accordance with IRC section 529 for qualified higher education expenses, as defined in IRC section 529. The CalKIDS program allows for an exclusion from gross income for funds deposited and investment returns accrued in a CalKIDS account. The CalKIDS program conforms to federal amendments to the IRC if the Scholarshare Investment Board determines that the IRC amendment is consistent with the purposes of the CalKIDS program. If the Scholarshare Investment Board determines that the amendment to the definition of qualified higher education expenses to include qualified postsecondary credentialing expenses as eligible for an IRC section 529 distribution furthers the purposes of the CalKIDS program, the board may conform to those provisions.

Revenue Impact

The estimated revenue impact to conform to the above provision would result in the following loss:

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70415, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Modification of excise tax on investment income of certain private colleges and universities
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
The provision applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
4968, 6033
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
N/A
Summary of Federal Change

Previously, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 13701) added a federal law that imposed an excise tax on an applicable educational institution for each taxable year equal to 1.4 percent of the net investment income of the institution for the taxable year.

This provision replaces the 1.4 percent excise tax with a tiered percentage of the net investment income of the institution for the taxable year based on an institution’s student adjusted endowment amounts as follows:

  • 1.4 percent for an institution with a student adjusted endowment of at least $500,000 and not in excess of $750,000,
  • 4 percent for an institution with a student adjusted endowment in excess of $750,000 and not in excess of $2,000,000 and
  • 8 percent for an institution with a student adjustment endowment in excess of $2,000,000.

This provision also modifies the definition of an applicable educational institution as an institution: (1) that has at least 3,000 (previously 500) students during the preceding taxable year; (2) that is an eligible educational institution as described in section 25A of the IRC; (3) that is not described in the first section of section 511(a)(2)(B) of the IRC (generally describing State colleges and universities); (4) has student adjusted endowments of at least $500,000; and (5) more than 50 percent of the students of which are located in the United States. For this purpose, the number of students at a location is based on the daily average number of full-time students attending the institution, with part-time students being taken into account on a full-time student equivalent basis.

The excise tax is calculated as a percent of net investment income and is determined using rules similar to the rules of IRC section 4940(c) (relating to the net investment income of a private foundation). The provision provides that the computation of net investment income includes student loan interest and federally subsidized royalty income.

For purposes of determining whether an institution meets the student adjusted endowment asset threshold and determining net investment income, assets and net investment income include amounts with respect to an organization that is related to the institution. An organization is treated as related to the institution for this purpose if the organization: (1) controls, or is controlled by, the institution; (2) is controlled by one or more persons that control the institution; or (3) is a supported organization or a supporting organization during the taxable year with respect to the institution. In addition, (1) no such amount is taken into account with respect to more than one educational institution; and (2) unless the related organization is controlled by the educational institution or is a supporting organization (described in IRC section 509(a)(3)) with respect to the institution for the taxable year, assets and investment income that are not intended or available for the use or benefit of the educational institution are not taken into account.

The provision provides that the Secretary would promulgate regulations or other guidance necessary to prevent avoidance of the tax under this provision, including regulations or other guidance to prevent tax avoidance by restructuring of endowment funds or other arrangements to reduce or eliminate net investment income.

The provision would additionally require each applicable educational institution exempt from taxation under IRC section 501(a) to include on its annual return the number of tuition-paying students taken into account for purposes of the excise tax and the number of students of the institution calculated in accordance with the excise tax.

California Impact

The FTB does not administer these types of excise taxes.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70416, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Expanding application of tax on excess compensation within tax-exempt organizations
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
The provision applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
4960
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
N/A
Summary of Federal Change

Previously, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 13602) added a federal law that imposes an excise tax on an applicable tax-exempt organization for remuneration paid to covered employees computed on the remuneration paid in excess of $1 million, plus any excess parachute payments. Specifically, the excise tax is equal to 21 percent, and is imposed on (1) remuneration (excluding any excess parachute payment) paid in any taxable year by an applicable tax-exempt organization to a covered employee that exceeds $1 million, plus (2) any excess parachute payment paid by an applicable tax-exempt organization to any covered employee, as defined.

A covered employee was defined as any current or former employee of an applicable tax-exempt organization if the employee is (1) one of the five highest compensated employees of the organization for the tax year, or (2) was a covered employee of the organization, or any predecessor of the organization.

This provision modifies the definition of covered employee to provide that the excise tax applies to any employee, including any former employee who was an employee of the organization, or of a predecessor organization, during any taxable year beginning after December 31, 2016.

California Impact

The FTB does not administer these types of excise taxes.

Relevant RTC Sections
17053.73, 18631, 23626
Summary of Federal Change

Qualified Opportunity Zones Designations:

This provision permanently extends the Opportunity Zone program to provide a rolling 10-year period of Opportunity Zone designations beginning January 1 following the date on which the qualified opportunity zones were certified and designated by the Secretary.

This provision modifies the definition of “low-income community” to mean any population census tract if:

  • Such population has a median family income that does not exceed 70 percent of the statewide median family income for census tracts outside a metropolitan area or does not exceed 70 percent of the median family income of the metropolitan area if located within a metropolitan area, or
  • Such population tract has a poverty rate of at least 20 percent and has a median family income that does not exceed 125 percent of the statewide median family income for census tracts outside a metropolitan area or does not exceed 125 percent of the median family income of the metropolitan area if located within a metropolitan area.

This provision also repeals the rules related to the designation of tracts contiguous with low-income communities established under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Public Law 115-97, section 13823).

The provision also repeals the special rule for Puerto Rico established under the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018 (Public Law 115-123, section 41115).

Special Rules for Capital Gains Invested in Opportunity Zones:

These provisions modify the special rules for capital gains invested in opportunity zones under IRC section 1400Z-2. Generally, a taxpayer may elect to exclude from gross income the gain from a sale to, or exchange with, an unrelated person of any property held by a taxpayer as long as the gain does not exceed the aggregate amount invested by the taxpayer in a qualified opportunity fund during a 180-day period beginning on the date of such sales. The provision modifies the year of inclusion on the deferral of such gain to either the earlier date on which such an investment is sold or exchanged or 5 years after the date of the investment in the qualified opportunity fund.

Generally, a taxpayer’s basis in their investment in a qualified opportunity zone held for 5 years is increased by 10 percent of the amount of the gain deferred pursuant to IRC section 1400Z-2 before inclusion of the deferred gain in gross income. The provision provides an increase to a taxpayer’s basis by 30 percent if their investment in a qualified opportunity zone held for 5 years, was an investment in a “qualified rural opportunity fund.”

The provision adds and defines the term “qualified rural opportunity fund” as a qualified opportunity fund that holds at least 90 percent of its assets in qualified opportunity property which is either (1) a qualified opportunity zone business property used is an opportunity zone comprised entirely of a rural area or (2) a qualified opportunity zone stock or qualified opportunity zone partnership interest in which the intangible property owned or leased is qualified opportunity zone property and is used in an opportunity zone comprised entirely of a rural area. The term “rural area” means any area other than a city or town that has a population greater than 50,000 and any urbanized area contiguous and adjacent to a city or town that has a population greater than 50,000.

This provision also modifies the special rules for investments held for at least 10 years related to the basis of such investment and removes the special rules for investments held for at least 7 years.

The provision also modifies the required percentage increase of the adjusted basis of property located in qualified opportunity zone comprised entirely of a rural area, from 100 percent to 50 percent, to be considered substantial improvement.

Filing Requirements for Qualified Opportunity Funds and Qualified Rural Opportunity Funds:

This provision will require every qualified opportunity fund to file an annual return with the Secretary and provide information about the qualified opportunity fund, including but not limited to name, address, TIN, organization type, and value of total assets and property, in the manner as prescribed by the Secretary. Any person required to file an annual return with the Secretary must furnish a statement to the investors. This provision will also require every applicable qualified opportunity zone business and qualified rural opportunity zone business to provide a written statement to the qualified opportunity fund disclosing any information prescribed by the Secretary. The term “applicable qualified opportunity zone business” means a trade of business of a qualified opportunity fund in which such fund holds qualified zone stock or a qualified opportunity zone partnership interest.

This provision also adds failure to comply with information reporting requirements penalties for any person required to file an annual return on behalf of a qualified fund under IRC section 6039K.

California Impact

California does not conform to the deferral and exclusion of capital gains reinvested or invested in qualified opportunity zone funds under IRC sections 1400Z-1 and 1400Z-2 and does not conform to the changes made by OBBBA to these provisions.

California law provides, under the AFITL, that the FTB may require a copy of any information return required to be filed with the Secretary of the Treasury and enacted on or after January 1, 2009, at the time and in the form and manner as the FTB may, by forms and instructions, require.

California does not conform to the new section that added information reporting requirements penalties for any person required to file an annual return on behalf of a qualified fund under IRC section 6039K. However, California has standalone penalties provisions that are imposed for the failure to file correction information returns and payee statements required under the AFITL. These penalties are determined in accordance with IRC sections 6721 and 6722.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Title

Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025

The increase in the state housing credit ceiling is applicable for taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025. The change in the special rule for tax exempt bond financing is applicable for buildings placed in service in taxable years beginning after 12/31/2025.

42
California Conforms?
Yes

Summary of Federal Change

The provision permanently increases a state’s housing credit ceiling for the low-income housing credit (LIHC) for calendar years beginning after December 31, 2025.

This provision modifies the special rule for a building financed with tax exempt bonds, to allow the LIHC without regard to the amount allocated for a building if:

  • 50 percent or more the aggregate basis of such a building and the land on which the building is located is financed by 1 or more obligations where interest from a private activity bond (IRC section 146) or state or local bond (IRC section 103) is exempt from taxation, or
  • 25 percent or more the aggregate basis of such building and the land on which the building is located is financed by 1 or more obligations where interest from a private activity bond (IRC section 146) or state or local bond (IRC section 103) is exempt from taxation, was issued after December 31, 2025 and provided the financing is not less than 5 percent of the aggregate basis of such building and land.

For purposes of applying the special rule for a building financed with tax exempt bonds, any rehabilitation expenditure of a building that is treated as a separate new building, both the existing building and the new building shall be treated as being placed in service on the close of the 24-month period under IRC section 42(e)(4).

California Impact

Under the PITL and CTIL, California generally conforms by reference to the LIHC, with modifications, such as:

  • Rents must be maintained at low-income levels for 30 years (15 years for federal), and
  • CTCAC must have authorized a federal credit to the taxpayer, or the taxpayer must qualify for the federal credit.

California law conforms by reference to the changes made by this provision.

California Conforms?

Summary of Federal Change

A taxpayer other than a corporation can exclude a percentage of the gain from the sale of certain qualified small business stock (QSBS) acquired at original issue and held for at least five years.

Under prior federal law, the amount of gain eligible for the exclusion by an individual with respect to the stock of any corporation was the greater of (1) ten times the taxpayer’s basis in the stock or (2) $10 million (reduced by the amount of gain eligible for exclusion in prior years). Also under prior federal law, to qualify as a small business, when the stock was issued, the aggregate gross assets (i.e., cash plus aggregate adjusted basis of other property) held by the corporation could not exceed $50 million. Different percentages applied depending on whether the QSBS was in an empowerment zone business or on the date of acquisition.

This provision creates new thresholds related to the percentage of the gain eligible for the gross income exclusion when the stock is held for at least 3 years. The eligible percentages are as follows:

  • 50% when stock is held for 3 years
  • 75% when held for 4 years, and
  • 100% when held for 5 years or more

In addition, this provision modifies the applicable dollar limitation on eligible gain from one or more dispositions of stock for the taxable year, from $10 million to $15 million, for stock acquired after July 4, 2025. Additionally, this provision increases the aggregate gross asset limitation from $50 million to $75 million. These modified limitations are to be adjusted annually by inflation beginning in 2027.

California Impact

California does not conform to the federal small business stock exclusion. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

Under the CTL, California does not conform to federal MACRS depreciation. Instead, the CTL is generally in substantial conformity to the pre-1981 federal asset depreciation range (ADR) rules, which generally allow property to be depreciated based on its useful life. The CTL does not conform to this provision.

Additionally, under the PITL and the CTL, California does not conform to the federal election to deduct the cost of any qualifying film and television production in the year the expenditure is incurred in lieu of capitalizing the cost and recovering it through depreciation allowances. Instead, under both the PITL and the CTL, California generally conforms to the federal income-forecast method to determine the depreciation recovery periods of property such as films, videotapes, television, book rights, patents, master sound recordings, video games, and like items. Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70435, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Exclusion of interest on loans secured by rural or agricultural real property
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Taxable years ending after 07/04/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
139L, affecting 265
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17131, 17280
Summary of Federal Change

The provision would exclude from gross income 25 percent of the interest received by a qualified lender on any qualified real estate loan.

The provision defines “qualified lender” as (1) any bank or savings association with deposits insured under the Federal Deposit Insurance Act; (2) any State or federally regulated insurance company; (3) any entity wholly owned, directly or indirectly, by a company that is treated as a bank holding company for purposes of section 8 of the International Banking Act of 1978 ; (4) any entity wholly owned, directly or indirectly, by a company that is considered an insurance holding company under the laws of any State; and (5) with respect to interest received on a qualified real estate loan secured by real property substantially used for the production of agricultural products, any federally chartered instrumentality of the United States established under section 8.1(a) of the Farm Credit Act of 1971.

For entities under (3) and (4), above, the entity must be organized, incorporated, or established under the laws of the United States or any State and its principal place of business is in the United States or any territory of the United States.

The provision defines “qualified real estate loan” as any loan secured by rural or agricultural real estate or a leasehold mortgage on rural or agricultural real estate that is made to a person other than a specified foreign entity after July 4, 2025. For refinancings, a loan would not be treated as made after July 4, 2025, if the proceeds of the loan are used to refinance a loan that was made on or before July 4, 2025.

The provision defines “rural or agricultural real estate” as any real property which is substantially used for the production of one or more agricultural products, any real property which is substantially used in the trade or business of fishing or seafood processing, and any aquaculture facility. Aquaculture facility is defined as any land, structure or other appurtenance used for aquaculture, and includes any hatchery, rearing pond, raceway, pen, or incubator. Rural or agricultural real estate does not include any property not located in a State or a possession of the United States.

The provision provides a coordination rule with IRC section 265, which provides requirements for expenses and interest related to tax exempt income and generally disallows a deduction for interest on indebtedness that is excluded from tax. Under this rule, 25 percent of the interest on indebtedness of a qualified real estate loan would not be deductible and the basis would be reduced by 25 percent.

California Impact

Under the CLT, California does not conform to IRC 139L, relating to interest on loans secured by rural or agricultural real property. Additionally, California does not conform to IRC section 265, regarding expenses and interest relating to tax-exempt income, but instead has stand-alone language that disallows certain deductions related to income not included in the measure of tax.

As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

Revenue Impact

The estimated revenue impact to conform to the above federal provisions would result in the following loss:

($5,000,000) ($4,600,000) ($5,800,000) ($7,300,000)

Summary of Federal Change

This provision adds a new section that redesignates current IRC section 1062 as IRC section 1063. This provision would allow, in the case of gain from the sale or exchange of qualified farmland property to a qualified farmer, at the election of the taxpayer, the portion of the net income tax of such taxpayer for the taxable year of the sale or exchange which is equal to the applicable net tax liability to be paid in 4 equal installments over four years.

An election to pay tax in installments must be made by the due date for the return of tax for the taxable year in which the gain from the sale or exchange of qualified farmland property to a qualified farmer occurs, without regard to extensions. The first installment would be required to be paid on the due date for the return of tax for the taxable year in which the gain occurs and each succeeding installment would be required to be paid on the due date of the return for the taxable year following the year that the preceding installment was made.

In the case of a sale or exchange by a partnership or S corporation, the election is made at the partner or shareholder level. The Secretary could prescribe regulations for purposes of the election.

If the taxpayer fails to timely pay any installment, the unpaid portion of any remaining installments becomes due on the date of the failure. If the taxpayer dies, then the unpaid portion of any remaining installments becomes due on the date of the return for the taxable year in which the taxpayer dies.

For a C corporation, trust, or estate, if there is a liquidation or sale of substantially all the assets of the taxpayer, a cessation of business by the taxpayer (in the case of a C corporation), or any similar circumstance, then the unpaid portion of all remaining installments is due on the date of such event (or the day before the petition is filed in a Title 11 or similar case). However, this would not apply if the sale of substantially all the assets of a taxpayer is to a buyer who enters into an agreement with the Secretary making the buyer liable for the remaining installments due in the same manner as if the buyer were the taxpayer.

This provision would also require the proration of installments if a deficiency is assessed with respect to the tax liability from the gain. The prorated portion of the installment that is not currently due would be due at the same time as such installment and the prorated portion of an installment that was already due would be paid upon notice and demand. However, the installments would not be prorated if the deficiency was due to negligence, intentional disregard, or fraud.

The provision defines “qualified farmland property” as real property located in the United States that has been used by the taxpayer as a farm for farming purposes or leased by the taxpayer to a qualified farmer for farming purposes, during substantially all of the 10-year period ending on the date of the qualified sale or exchange, and which is subject to a covenant or other legally enforceable restriction which prohibits the use of such property other than as a farm for farming purposes for any period before the date that is 10 years after the date of the sale or exchange. Property that is used or leased by a partnership or S corporation would be treated as used or leased by each person who holds a direct or indirect interest in the partnership or S corporation.

The provision defines “qualified farmer” as any individual who is actively engaged in farming within the meaning of subsections (b) and (c) of section 1001 of the Food Security Act of 1986.

The terms farm and farming purposes have the same meanings as defined under IRC 2032A(e).

California Impact

California conforms by reference to Subchapter O of Chapter 1 of Subtitle A of the IRC, relating to gain or loss on disposition of property, as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, in RTC section 18031. As a result, California would not conform to these provisions.

Revenue Impact

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70438, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Extension of rules for treatment of certain disaster-related personal casualty losses
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
Personal casualty losses arising in a qualified disaster area that was declared between 01/01/2020, and 09/02/2025, with the incident period of that related qualified disaster beginning on or after 12/28/2019 and before 08/03/25.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
Uncodified, affecting Consolidated Appropriation Acts, 2021, PL 116-260, Section 301, Division EE - Taxpayer Certainty and Disaster Tax Relief Act of 2020
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
17201, 17204
Summary of Federal Change

The Taxpayer Certainty and Disaster Tax Relief Act (TCDTRA) of 2020 (part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 (CAA, 2021), Public Law (P.L.) 116-260), provides special rules for individuals who had qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses in a Presidentially declared disaster area, that was declared a major disaster on or after January 1, 2020 and on or before February 25, 2021. The relief applied to disasters with an incident period beginning on or after December 28, 2019, and on or before December 27, 2020.

The Federal Disaster Tax Relief Act (FDTRA) of 2023 (P.L. 118-148) extended the disaster relief treatment for personal casualty losses provided under the TCDTRA to include Presidentially declared disasters that are declared a major disaster on or before February 10, 2025, with an incident period beginning on or after December 28, 2019, and on or before December 12, 2024.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) of 2025 extends the disaster relief treatment for personal casualty losses provided under the TCDTRA to September 2, 2025. The relief applies to disasters with an incident period beginning on or after December 28, 2019, and on or before July 4, 2025.

California Impact

Under the PITL, California generally conforms to IRC section 165 as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, and specifically does not conform to the special rules for individuals who had qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses arising in a qualified disaster area, as provided in the TCDTRA of 2020. As a result, California law does not conform to the changes of this provision extending the special rules for qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses arising in a qualified disaster area.

Revenue Impact
N/A

This provision would increase the percentage of a real estate investment trust’s (REIT) total assets that may be represented by securities of one or more taxable REIT subsidiaries from 20 percent to 25 percent.

California Impact

California generally conforms to federal REIT rules as of the specified date of January 1, 2025, with modifications. However, California law provides that a corporation, trust, or association that is a REIT for any taxable year for federal purposes is automatically a REIT for California purposes for the same taxable year. Conversely, a corporation, trust, or association that is a not a REIT for any taxable year for federal purposes is automatically not a REIT for California purposes for the same taxable year.

Although California does not conform to the change made by this act, under California law, for any taxable year that a trust qualifies for REIT status for federal purposes is determinative for California purposes. Thus, any trust that qualifies as a REIT for federal purposes will automatically qualify as a REIT for California purposes.

Summary of Federal Change

IRC section 45

This provision expands the 10 percent increase in the renewable electricity production credit to advanced nuclear facilities located in a metropolitan statistical area which has (or, at any time during the period beginning after December 31, 2009, had) 0.17 percent or greater direct employment related to the advancement of nuclear power.

IRC section 45Y

The provision terminates the clean electricity production credit for qualified wind and solar facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027. Additionally, a qualified facility that begins construction after December 31, 2025, that receives material assistance from prohibited foreign entities is ineligible for the tax credit. No credit is allowed to a specified foreign entity or foreign-influenced entity. The provision also prohibits the clean electricity production credit for the production of electricity with respect to qualified solar water heating property or qualified small wind energy property, as defined in IRC section 25D(d)(1) and (4), respectively, that are leased to a third party during the taxable year. The provision modifies the credit phase out.

IRC section 6418

A taxpayer is prohibited from transferring eligible energy credits as a payment against income tax to a specified foreign entity as defined.

IRC section 6501

The provision extends the statute of limitations to assess a deficiency for an underpayment of tax as a result of an error in the determination of whether a taxpayer received “material assistance from a prohibited foreign entity,” to 6 years after the return for that year was filed.

IRC section 6662

The provision modifies the definition of what is a substantial understatement for the accuracy-related penalty from 10 percent of the tax required on the return to 1 percent when the understatement is based on the disallowance of the following applicable energy credits: advanced manufacturing production credit, clean electricity production credit, and clean electricity investment credit.

IRC section 6695B

This provision adds section 6695B, which imposes a new penalty for providing an inaccurate or false certification with respect to a manufactured product, eligible component, or constituent element, material, or subcomponent of an eligible component related to the construction of a qualified facility or energy storage technology that results in the disallowance of the advanced manufacturing production credit, clean electricity production credit, or clean electricity investment credit that exceeds the lesser of 5 percent of the tax required to be reported on the return or $100,000.

IRC section 7701

This provision adds definitions of the terms “prohibited foreign entities” as a “foreign-influenced entity,” or a “specified foreign entity,” which includes a “foreign-controlled entity” and material assistance from a prohibited foreign entity.

The provision provides that the sustainable aviation fuel credit would no longer apply to any sale or use for any period after September 30, 2025. This provision retroactively applies to fuel sold before July 4, 2025, but only to the extent that credits claimed have not been paid or allowed as of July 4, 2025.

Biodiesel and renewable diesel use as fuel (IRC section 40A and IRC section 6418)

The provision increases the amount of small agri-biodiesel producer credit and allows the credit in addition to any applicable clean fuel production credit. The provision (IRC section 6418) also allows the small agri-biodiesel producer credit to be transferred to an unrelated taxpayer. This provision modifies the definition of qualifying income for publicly traded partnerships to be exempt from treatment as a corporation under the IRC. The term “qualifying income” is modified to include income and gains derived from:

  • The transportation or storage of sustainable aviation fuel and liquified or compressed hydrogen,
  • The generation, availability for such generation, or storage of electric power, or the capture of carbon dioxide, at a qualified facility where not less than 50 percent of the total carbon oxide production is qualified carbon oxide production without regard to any required construction date,
  • The production of electricity from any advanced nuclear facility,
  • The production of electricity or thermal energy exclusively from geothermal or qualified hydropower production
  • The operation of energy property which includes equipment, used to produce, distribute, or use energy from a geothermal deposit, but only with respect to electricity generated by geothermal power up to the electrical transmission stage, or equipment which uses the ground or ground water as a thermal energy source to heat a structure or as a thermal energy sink to cool a structure, without regard to any required construction date.
California Impact

Under the PITL, California law automatically conforms to the federal definition of “qualifying income” for determining whether a publicly traded partnerships is treated as a corporation. As a result, California conforms under the PITL to the changes made by this provision.

Under the CTL, California conforms with modifications to certain publicly traded partnerships treated as corporations as of the “specified date” of January 1, 2025. As a result, California does not conform under the CTL to the changes made by this provision.

Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section

California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections

Summary of Federal Change

The provision would make permanent the business loss limitation, restricting a non-corporate taxpayer’s losses to $250,000 ($500,000 in the case of a joint return) beginning after taxable year December 31, 2026. Excess business losses are disallowed for the taxable year and are carried forward and treated as part of the taxpayer's net operating loss (NOL) carryforward in the following taxable years. An excess business loss for the taxable year is the excess of total deductions of the taxpayer attributable to the taxpayer's trades and businesses, over the sum of aggregate gross income or gain of the taxpayer plus a threshold amount.

The provision would also modify the adjustment for inflation for any taxable year beginning after December 31, 2025, and the cost-of-living adjustment to calendar year 2024.

California Impact

Under the PITL and CTL, California conforms to IRC section 461 as of January 1, 2025. Under the PITL, California has modified conformity to IRC section 461(l), relating to limitation on excess business losses on noncorporate taxpayers, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2018. For California purposes, losses are treated as an excess business loss carryover to the following taxable year as opposed to a net operating loss carryover under IRC section 172. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

Title

Background

IRC Section

California Conforms?

Summary of Federal Change

This provision extends the $1,000,000 deduction limitation for compensation paid to a “specified covered employee,” of a controlled group that includes a publicly held corporation. A controlled group is defined as a group treated as a single employer under a controlled group of corporations (IRC section 414(b)), partnerships and proprietorships (IRC section 414(c)), an affiliated service group (IRC section 414(m)), or under the Secretary of the Treasury regulations (IRC section 414(o)). A “specified covered employee” is defined as any of the following:

  • A principal executive officer or the principal financial officer of the publicly held corporation.
  • The three most highly compensated officers of the publicly held corporation for the taxable year (other than the principal executive officer or principal financial officer) who are required to be reported under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
  • A former employee of the publicly held corporation described above in any preceding taxable year beginning after December 31,2016.
  • The five highest compensated employees of all members of the controlled group other than the individuals described above.

In determining the amount members of a controlled group are limited from deducting all compensation paid to a specified covered employee by a member of the controlled group would be aggregated. Amounts in excess of $1,000,000 would be proportioned to each controlled group member based on the portion of compensation paid by that member.

California Impact

California conforms, with modifications, to the federal treatment of certain excessive employee remuneration under IRC section 162 as of the specified date of January 1, 2025. Additionally, under the PITL, California does not conform to the limitation on excessive employee remuneration to the five highest compensated employees. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made under this provision to extend the $1,000,000 deduction limitation to the controlled group.

Details of Public Law 119-21, section 70605, One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Title
One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Enforcement provisions with respect to COVID-related employee retention credits
Fed Effective Date
07/04/2025
Fed Operative Date
This provision applies to aid, assistance, and advice provided, or assessments made, or claims for credit or refund made, after 07/04/2025.
Background
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
IRC Section
3134 and 6676, and uncodified sections affecting IRC sections 52, 414, 3134, 6201, 6511, 6695, 6676, and 7705
California Conforms?
No
Relevant RTC Sections
N/A
Summary of Federal Change

The Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act (CARES Act, P.L. 116-136) created a refundable payroll tax credit known as the Employee Retention Tax Credit (ERTC) that was applied against applicable employment taxes. ERTC provided COVID-19 relief to employers whose operations were impacted by the shutdown.

This provision provides that any COVID-ERTC promoter who does not comply with the due diligence requirements (with respect to determining eligibility for the ERTC would be required to pay a penalty of $1,000 for each instance of noncompliance. The $1,000 penalty would be treated as a penalty imposed by the Secretary in the same manner taxes are assessed.

A “COVID-ERTC promoter” is defined as, any person who provides aid, assistance, or advice with respect to any COVID–ERTC document if, the person charges a fee based on the credit amount or refund and 20 percent or more of the person’s gross receipts are from ERTC-related services, or 50 percent or more of the person’s gross receipts are from ERTC-related services, or 20 percent or more of the person’s gross receipts are from ERTC-related services and the person’s gross receipts exceed $500,000.

A “COVID-ERTC promoter” does not include a certified professional employer organization.

A “COVID-ERTC Document” is defined as any return, affidavit, claim or other document related to eligibility for, or the calculation or determination of any amount directly related to any such credit or advance payment.

The provision specifies that no credit will be allowed and no refund is to be made after July 4, 2025, unless that claim for a credit or refund was filed by the taxpayer prior to January 31, 2024. Additionally, the statute of limitations on the assessment of amounts related to the ERTC would be extended to six years from the date the credit or claim for refund is made and this extension would also apply an assessment related to the wage deduction used to calculate the credit.

The provision expands the penalty for erroneous claim for refund or credit to also apply to excessive claims for refund or credit of employment tax.

The Secretary is required to issue regulations or other guidance that may be needed or appropriate to carry out the purpose of this provision.

California Impact

The FTB does not administer employment taxes and the changes made by this provision do not impact the department. Employment taxes are administered by the Employment Development Department.

Revenue Impact
N/A

Summary of Federal Change

Under federal law, eligible individuals may establish a Health Savings Account (HSA), which provides tax-favored treatment for current medical expenses, as well as the ability to save on a tax-favored basis for future medical expenses. Generally, individuals are eligible to establish an HSA when they are covered by a high-deductible health plan and have no other health coverage (with the exception of plans providing certain permitted benefits/coverage). A high-deductible health plan is permitted to provide telehealth and other remote care services without satisfaction of the plan’s minimum deductible. This means a health plan is still considered a high-deductible health plan even if it fails to require a deductible for telehealth and other remote care services for those plan years. Prior to this act, this law was set to expire for plan years beginning before January 1, 2025. This provision makes permanent the safe harbor rules that allow plans to include telehealth services absent a required deductible.

California Impact

California specifically does not conform to federal HSAs and does not conform to the safe harbor for the absence of a deductible for telehealth and other remote care services. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

Summary of Federal Change

Under federal law, eligible individuals may establish a Health Savings Account (HSA), which provides tax-favored treatment for current medical expenses, as well as the ability to save on a tax-favored basis for future medical expenses. Generally, individuals are eligible to establish an HSA when they are covered by a high-deductible health plan and have no other health coverage (with the exception of plans providing certain permitted benefits/coverage).

Federal law, under the Affordable Care Act (Public Law 111-148, Section 1302), provided categories of plans with set employer and employee shared costs. The plans include the following levels, bronze, silver, gold, or platinum, and catastrophic. A bronze plan requires that employers provide a level of benefit coverage at 60% with the employee paying the remainder. A catastrophic plan is available when no other plans are made available and the employee is under 30 years old with income hardships. This provision would allow bronze and catastrophic level plans to be classified as high-deductible health plans for purposes of establishing HSAs, for months beginning after December 31, 2025.

California Impact

California specifically does not conform to federal HSAs and does not conform to the Bronze and Catastrophic level plans classification as high-deductible health plans. As a result, California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

Under federal law, eligible individuals may establish a Health Savings Account (HSA), which provides tax-favored treatment for current medical expenses, as well as the ability to save on a tax-favored basis for future medical expenses. Generally, individuals are eligible to establish an HSA when they are covered by a high-deductible health plan and have no other health coverage (with the exception of plans providing certain permitted benefits/coverage). Summary of Federal Change

This provision allows the Secretary to postpone federal tax deadlines upon the written request of a Governor of a State (or Mayor in the case of the District of Columbia) to when there is a qualified state declared disaster. A qualified state declared disaster is defined as any natural catastrophe (including any hurricane, tornado, storm, high water, wind-driven water, tidal wave, tsunami, earthquake, volcanic eruption, landslide, mudslide, snowstorm, or drought), or, regardless of cause, any fire, flood, or explosion, in any part of the State, that the Governor of such State (or the Mayor in the case of the District of Columbia) determines causes damage to require a postponement of tax deadlines.

This provision also defines a state to include the District of Columbia, Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.

This section revises the mandatory filing deadline extension to 120 days instead of 60 days, for certain acts, such as filing a tax return, paying income tax, filing a claim for refund, or filing a petition with a Tax Court. The extension applies for qualified taxpayers affected by federally declared disasters 120 days after the later of the earliest incident or the date the declaration was issued. If there are multiple declarations issued within the 120-day period, a separate period for each declaration will be determined using the later of: 1) the earliest incident or 2) the date the declaration was issued.

California Impact

California conforms by reference with modifications to IRC section 7508A, relating to postponement of certain tax-related deadlines. Under California law, the Director of Finance has the authority to determine whether a taxpayer is affected by a state of emergency, and whether state tax deadlines should be postponed due to a state of emergency. California law provides impacted taxpayers with postponement of tax-related deadlines, as prescribed by the Secretary under IRC section 7508A, an additional relief period that begins on the date the state postponement period expires, if any, and ends on the date the federal postponement period expires.

Title
Internal Revenue Service Math and Taxpayer Help Act, Improvement of notices of math or clerical error
Fed Effective Date

Background
Internal Revenue Service Math and Taxpayer Help Act
IRC Section

California Conforms?

Summary of Federal Change

This provision requires additional information on the notice that taxpayers receive when a mathematical or clerical error occurs on their tax return. The notice would be required to be sent to the taxpayer’s last known address, and includes the following:

  • a plain language explanation of the mathematical or clerical error,
  • an itemized mathematical computation of direct or incidental adjustments made on the return in correction of the error,
  • contact information for the automated phone transcript service, and
  • the date the taxpayer can request an abatement for the assessment.

This provision requires additional information to be provided if the taxpayer requests an abatement within 60 days and if the Secretary of the Treasury determines the adjustment can be abated, the notice of abatement must include the following:

  • Be sent to the taxpayer’s last known address,
  • Describe the abatement in comprehensive, plain language, and
  • Provide an itemized mathematical computation of adjustments made to items in the mathematical or clerical error notice.

The provision also requires the Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the National Taxpayer Advocate, to implement a pilot program to send a trial number of notices of mathematical or clerical error by certified or registered mail with e-signature confirmation of receipt. It also requires a report to Congress on the type of error to which the notices relate on the number of math or clerical errors noticed, the dollar amounts, the number of abatements, and the effect of the pilot program on taxpayer response and adjustments to abatements to tax.

California Impact

California does not conform to IRC section 6213 but instead has a standalone law for notices and assessments related to math errors. The FTB issues a Notice of Tax Return Change (NTRC) when an error is identified on a taxpayer’s tax return. The NTRC will contain information, such as:

  • The change made to the return,
  • Any action the taxpayer may take whether they agree or disagree with the correction,
  • A plain language explanation of the change, which may include taxpayer’s calculation and the FTB’s calculation,
  • How to contact the FTB.

California does not conform to the changes made by this provision.

Summary of Federal Change

Under the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (also called the Affordable Care Act, or ACA, Public Law 111-148), individuals, including their dependents, must be covered by a health plan that provides at least minimum essential coverage (commonly referred to as the “individual mandate”) or be subject to a tax (also referred to as the Individual Shared Responsibility (ISR) penalty) for failure to maintain the coverage. Under the ACA, employers are required to provide the following forms to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and the individual:

  • Form 1095-B – Health Coverage, which reports information to the IRS and taxpayers who have minimum essential coverage.
  • Form 1095-C – Employer-Provided Health Insurance Offer and Coverage, which reports information to the IRS and full-time employees of a large employer who work for one month or more of the calendar year for the employer detailing their health coverage enrollment and offers for their employees.

The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA, Public Law 115-97, section 11081) reduced the amount of the Individual Shared Responsibility (ISR) penalty to zero with respect to health coverage status for months beginning after December 31, 2018. When the TCJA removed the ISR penalty, federal regulations (Treasury Regulations section 1.6055-1(g)(4)(B)) were put in place for employers to provide an alternative employee notification for Form 1095-B, only for those employees whose minimum essential health care coverage is zero and if mailed to the employee’s last known permanent address, or temporary address if no permanent address is known. However, Form 1095-C was still required to be sent to employees.

This provision allows employers to provide alternate employee notification for copies of Forms 1095-B and 1095-C. It is codifying the federal regulations providing for Form 1095-B requirements and extending the same treatment to Form 1095-C. Notification is considered timely when the employer posts in a clear, conspicuous and accessible manner for the individual to know how they can request a copy of these forms. If a copy is requested, it must be provided to the individual no later than January 31 of the following year the information return is required to be filed with the IRS or 30 days after the request is made, whichever is later.

Employers continue to be required to file these forms with the IRS.

California Impact

RTC section 18631(b) provides that a copy of certain federal information returns can be required to be filed with FTB at the time and in the manner as required by forms and instructions. As a result, California would conform to the changes requiring the information return related to Forms 1095-B and 1095-C.

Additionally, California has standalone sections imposing an Individual Shared Responsibility Penalty (Part 32 of the RTC) that is similar to the federal penalty. Under these rules, returns are required to be filed with the FTB, and written statements are required to be provided to individuals. Under RTC sections 61005(d) for returns filed with the FTB and (g) for written statements provided to individuals, a return that satisfies IRC section 6055 as in effect on December 15, 2017, meets the California reporting requirements. As a result, the new notification requirements under this provision would not be applicable for California purposes.

Summary of Federal Change

Under the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (also called the Affordable Care Act, or ACA, Public Law 111-148), individuals, including their dependents, must be covered by a health plan that provides at least minimum essential coverage (commonly referred to as the “individual mandate”) or be subject to a tax (also referred to as the individual shared responsibility (ISR) penalty) for failure to maintain the coverage.

An individual who has the minimum essential coverage will receive a copy of Form 1095-B – Health Coverage from government-sponsored programs, eligible employer-sponsored plans, individual market plans, and other coverage the Department of Health and Human Services designates. An employer with 50 or more employees (also known as an applicable large employer (ALE)) who offered enrollment in health care coverage will provide a copy of Form 1095-C – Employer Provided Health Insurance Offer and Coverage to their employees.
